JAZZ ORAL HISTORY PROJECT
George "Big Nick" Nicholas
Interviewed by
Dale Fitzgerald
Institute of Jazz Studies
March, 1980
Nick, we've talked a little bit before about your childhood, but there's still a lot to be said. You were born in Lansing, Michigan, in 1922; did you grow up there?

Yeah, I was born and raised there. What actually happened, from what I've heard, my mother and father separated after I was a baby and they went their separate ways. The last recollection I had was that I was with some people, my--supposedly--grandfather, in Ypsilanti, Michigan. I remember that. He was a preacher, and I used to go to church. And I became aware of music then, when I was four, I think. And finally my mother and father got back together. In 1928 I went to St. Louis with her. She had a beautiful voice. She loved music. And I became aware of music there (in St. Louis). I'll never forget, one day I went out in the street and I walked down the street and there was a band rehearsing and it was such a thrill. The back door was open and all the young children my age we were out there in the street and everybody was playing and it was a festive mood and I went back-door and it was just a marvelous thing to hear this band playing jazz music. And that was another impression on me. Then, after that, they sent me down to my grandmother in Charleston, South Carolina.
This was your father's mother or your mother's mother?

My father's mother. And I became aware of this. I'll never forget, every Saturday they would come around in the neighbourhood and give us tickets so that we could go up on Lincoln Avenue and see a movie free on Saturday. And then, another thing I remember, is that everybody could sing down there. And that impressed me. And everybody could dance. Everybody had rhythm. And I had a good time there; those are very fond memories. But, when I came back...oh, my mother came down to get me and I went back up to St. Louis with her again. We went to Jackson, Michigan, and I thought they were getting back together again. I'll never forget, my father had two brand new saxophones, saxophones, he had an alto and a tenor, in the house and it was 1930. They turned on the radio and I heard this wonderful music and it was jazz and I says "My goodness that sounds good." So I'll never forget the day he asked me could I blow these horns and I just tried and blow and I couldn't blow a note. That was my first introduction to the saxophone.
You were eight years old then?
Yeah. So that passed. So then

some things happened there and then finally they decided to get together again in Lansing, Michigan, in 1932. Then they decided to break up and when they broke up, that day, when I came home from school my father had got a player piano and the dishes were in the sink and she took the car and when I walked in the door he was playing this player piano and I says, 'Good gracious, that's music,' and then things began to sink in a little more. So we were washing dishes together and he tried to explain to me that Mamma's gone and she took the car and whatnot, but we gonna make it. So, one thing I was good at was atheletics, so that took my mind off a lot of things, you know when you're young and impressionable, you know these things leave these deep scars. But I was a basketball player and I was a track man, even at that age.
Let's go back a little bit here for a minute, I just want to get the sequence of this straight. Now, you were born in Lansing and shortly after you were born, your mother and father split up...?
Yeah.
Were they married in Lansing?
Yeah, married in Lansing...and they split up...
And your mother went to St. Louis?

No...I don't know where she went, but my father put me in a foster home so...one time I was in Cleveland and he said when he come to get me this woman had a racket. There was about eight or nine babies and I was skinny, I looked like I was gettin' ready to die... ha, ha, ha. So I don't remember anything, but this is what he told me, until I went to my grandfather's on my mother's side, Reverend Carr, in Ypsilanti.
About how old were you then?
I was about three or four years old.
So the foster home was before that, when you were really young?
Yeah, I didn't know nothing about that...
What were some of your actual first memories, like what comes to mind...
I remember that I was lonesome

and then I also remember that some of the people I was with were kind and some were cruel. So, that's a tremendous impression on ya, but I survived and gradually I began to lean toward music and I began to hear it in different instances, but as I said, as I got older I became athletic and I was a good basketball player and a good track man and that helped sustain me, ya follow me, before I really became dedicated to music. And I think that helped build my body and give me strength to carry on 'cause blowin' a horn is very hard. Yeah. It's your nerves, it's your stomach, it's your wind, it's your whole stamina.
I want to spend a little bit more time with some of the specifics, some of the details. Do you have memories of St. Louis? Do you remember being in St. Louis?

Oh sure, 'cause I remember my mother was a lively woman and, you know, they used to have parties and I used to hear the music and then I remember Ringling Brothers Circus and we sneaked in under the tent; then I remember tryin' to stand on my head out in the street. I was so big I could never...I was so heavy...there were boys who could stand on their head and do the back flip, but...then I remember the home brew beer. They'd have a big freezer and they'd have it in these tin buckets and when they wasn't anybody lookin' I'd sneak in there and get me a little sip of that home brew. Boy that was really sumpin'.
This was all in St. Louis?
Yeah, that was fun city in those days.
Was your mother remarried then?

No, no, no, no. She never remarried. But that was a fun time and, as I said, she was a lovely person and she loved life and I got a chance to see some of the reality of life at a very young age. And I remember.
What section of St. Louis did she live in and did she work?

She was a seamstress and then she made hats, from what I can remember, she was very creative and she worked in these dress shops and these hat shops and do that creative work and designs for hats. And from what I understand, from what she told me later in life, she was singing too in a night club. Yeah. She was supposed to go to Europe with Ethel Waters, but something happened, I don't know what happened, but she was on her way, she had a little professional experience.
I see. As a singer. But at the time you
didn't know anything about that?
No, she didn't say anything to me about it. You know, she wanted to see how I was gonna work out.
So how many years were you actually in St. Louis?
About two.
And then from there you went to your father's mother's in...
In Charleston, South Carolina.
How long were you there?

I was there about a year, I guess. I remember Charleston, everything was so festive and I'll never forget my mother, when she came to get me we went to a restaurant and we had some hoppin John peas and rice and I never ate so much in my life, ya know. Hahahaha. And everybody loved music in Charleston because ya know they had their Victrolas and what not, I could hear the music, ya know, and that was an influence on me, now that I look back, that was a part of makin' me a musician. Yeah.
Now with your father's people there, what work did they do, what was going on in their house?

My grandmother, she worked for this Greek family. I'll never forget, she took me by there one day, she had to clean up and she wanted me to help her and we cleaned up the bedroom and she lift up the pillows --this was for me--and there was his gun. I said, 'Ohhohhhh.' Hahahaha. Then they used to have the weekend parties and, we were poor, we used to go down to the coke...you know, they stoked the...I don't know what you call that...but anyway we'd pick up this half used coke and we'd use it for heat, you know.

That's the first time I ever ate catfish. I never did like catfish after that. I never did like it. No. Hoppin Johns and rice and catfish, oh boy. Mmmmmmmm mmmmmm. Oh, and then there was Jenkins Orphanage. Oh, I forgot about them. There was a orphanage; now there was an experience. The Jenkins Orphanage Band would come by, maybe once a month, and they'd pass the hat and I thought that was just wonderful. So now I almost forgot about that.
And that was in Charleston?
Yeah, and oh they were blowin', I'll tell you, they were tryin' to get that money and get...But the
people loved em...
Was this an outdoor kind of thing?
Yeah...
Like in a park or a picnic or...
No, they'd stop in the neighbourhood, you know, then they'd go to another neighbourhood and in this section everybody'd gather around and would listen. I remember that.
Now, you never had any brothers or sisters, but were there any kids of your age, relatives, that lived with you at all in Charleston or in St. Louis?

Oh, my uncle and my aunt, I didn't know too much, that was vague, but they were very nice, you know, but...hmmmm, my aunt's name was Rebecca and my uncle's name was Charles. They were very nice, I remember them. I'll never forget, I got in a fight one day and this great big guy, he said something, I took a swing at him, but he tricked me. When I swung he ducked and grabbed my legs--this was a trick--and I went down. Then he was right on top of me. And I was fightin' and battlin' and
and my aunt says, "You big bully, get off my nephew". Hahahaha. That was like in a courtyard in Catfish Row.
Did they live right there (Catfish Row)?

I don't know if it was Catfish Row, but it was the same setup, you know, they had the apartments around and in the center they had the square, you know, it was like Catfish Row, but I'm not sure if it was.
So let's see, that was a year in Charleston and then it was back to Jackson, Michigan, or to Lansing?

It was to Lansing and my father had rented a house and my mohter and they were supposed to get together again and they were together for a little while, then when--you know--she disappeared--you know--with the car and everything. When I came home from school the next day, that's when he had the player piano and was playin'. I look back on that, it was marvelous, for a man to have that kind of brain, so he didn't want me to come home sad, you dig what I mean. So I'll never forget that.
Now, what work did your father do?

He was one of the first colored men to be employed by the Bell Telephone System in Jackson, Michigan. He stayed there until he died. Yeah, one of the first employees of the Bell Telephone Company and I got pictures of him in 1927--like that--with all these employees in Jackson, Michigan.
And he never remarried as well?
Oh no, no, no, no. Uhuh.
Now had you gone to school at all before you came back there to Lansing? Had you gone to school in St. Louis?
Yeah, I went to school in St. Louis, I remember that, but everything was so jimble-jamble, I don't even know when I was in school or when I was out.
But when you got back to Lansing, then things settled down a little bit?
Yeah, settled down period.
Then, what grade did you start in there?
Oh, let's see...oh, shoot...I guess about sixth grade, yeah...or fourth or fifth grade...let's see...yeah about the fourth or fifth grade. I don't remember details back then.
How far was the school away from where you lived?
It wasn't too far, it was about ten minutes walk.
And you walked to school everyday...by yourself, with friends?
Yeah, sometimes, with neighbours and what not.
What are some of the things you remember about that school? What was going on, whether it was an experience that you...
Well, I went to class, you know what I mean, there wasn't much of a music program until I got to high school, but I was involved in music at home

when I started piano lessons at nine. So I went through the routine and I didn't become involved publicly at all... Oh, wait a minute, in Junior High School, yes, I became involved with it, I was into athletics then, by that time you know my father and I'd got settled and I became involved with basketball and track and the Junior High School Band and then the little weekend band and we'd play for dances and what not and that's when I really got started, really. That's when things started becoming firm and I became serious about what I wanted to be, you know, and my father, he never said anything, but he silently approved of everything I did, he never said anything, but he approved. So I knew I had his approval so he gave me my head to go on, because he knew I was into music. He loved music, and he saw that I loved music, well he saw that I wanted to be an athlete, because I was active. So he didn't say nothing.
What sports did you play?

Basketball and track. I loved both and I love basketball and track today. I was a high jumper and a hurdler and I was a forward and center on the basketball team. It was some tough days but I will never forget John Middlesworth, he was the high school

coach and advisor, of course in those days the coach...he was the coach of the basketball team, the track team...it was all in one. And Joe Byers who was the coach of the basketball team and the track team at Pattongill High School ...Junior High...I'll never forget, Joe Byers and I, we went to Battle Creek and, you know, I was scorin' a lot of points and there was a couple of other guys who was doin' very well and we won, you see. But it was rough. The team was out there and this guy Joe...I'll never forget him... he decided that he was gonna cause some trouble, so I'll never forget this as long as I live, so the rest of the guys on the team, everybody was scared, so Joe Byers took his coat off and I said, "I'm which ya", and we stood back to back at the door of the bus and they saw that so they didn't do nothin'. Haha. They gettin' ready to do sumthin' there, mad 'cause they lost. I'll never forget him.
(I'm with cha...)
Now at this same time, you had developed an interest in music. When was the first point in school that you were involved in that?

In Junior High School they had the band, you know, the concert band, and I played clarinet in that and we had our concerts and what not and then, natural- ly, in high school, along with playin' basketball and track,

I was in the marchin' band at football games, playing clarinet. And then we had a jazz band, you know, and then I workin' on the weekends, you know, on little outside jobs. Yeah, so I became involved then.
Let's see if I can get this straight. When you say you were working on the weekends on outside jobs, what kind of job was that?

Well, like you get a dance out to Round Lake, Saturday night, something like that. Then they want...'cause they knew we had a very good band, 'cause we were doing all of Glenn Miller's and Count Basie, 'cause they had stock arrangements of these things which you could buy and so we had a little something goin' for ourselves.
What was the composition of this band that played on weekends?
Ohh, like three trumpets, four saxophones...
Oh, the real thing...
Oh yeah, shoot yeah, we had the stock arrangements, you know, we'd buy 'em and we could
do a job, you know.
And were you all high school kids?
Yeah.
When did that start? This is something I'd like to get into in some detail.
Oh well, let's see, that started in around 1937. Yeah...
You were about 15 then...a Junior or Sophomore, something like that...?

Yeah. Yeah, Sophomore. Yeah, well, Sy Jenkins, he was a very energetic fellow and the whole family, they liked music. I remember his brother, he played a little trumpet, he didn't keep it up, and the other brother played drums. But Sy--I didn't realize this at the time--Sy he was a West Indian fellow and I didn't know anything about that and I knew I'd go by the house and his mother was so sweet to me and his brothers were so nice to me and they all loved music so and Sy ended up being a lieutenant in the service. He made a career out of it. But anyway, he had the band that would work on
weekends, you know, away from school. And then there was Howard Brockington in the band; he was my best friend in Lansing, you see. He played trumpet. And it was a nice little thing.
How did you first get in? Did you have to audition for this; was it set up in that way or were you around when it started?

Well, no. We were all in the neighbourhood and we all leaned toward dance music and jazz mainly and we wanted to play, you know what I mean. So that's how that happened because it was a small town, at that time.
So, do you remember did someone ask you to do it or were you among the people who first talked about it and were you a leader in the group?

No, no. Sy was older and it was his idea, but he could see that, you know, that I was, you know, 1936 I started listening to the programs from New York and Chu Berry and them and so everybody knew that I was going this way, so they say Nick had to be a part of it. You know, that was one of them things.
Yeah, if I remember, just about that period
of time, you had already started playing the clarinet in school?

Yeah. Yeah, well my father had one, an old Albert System around the house. He started me on the piano at nine, you see, and then he had an old Albert System clarinet around the house...he was very sophisticated, you know, he just laid it there, you know, so I picked it up and I started playin' it, you know, so he smiled...he didn't say nothin'...and then I went on into the school band. And then eventually he got me another clarinet and that's how that started. And I could read good, I always could read good.
Did he teach you how to read?
No, uhuh, he played by ear. He watched me, and he didn't say nothin'.
So they taught reading (in school)?

Oh, yeah. Well, I had piano; I had the foundation, all I had to do was learn the fingering of the clarinet, because I knew how to read. See the main thing is the mechanism of the clarinet. And then I had it made, you know.
You said it was Albert System?
Oh, that he had and then when I went into school and I told them, I said, "Look, they playin' Boehm System," and so he got me a Boehm System.
What's the difference in that?

Well it's the fingering, you know. Albert's System is a little different than the Boehm System which is...Albert's System is more difficult to play. Barney Bigard played Albert System. But Boehm System is a little easier to play, the fingering and the comfort, etcetera. Yeah.
Allright, so when you entered the band, you entered the band playing clarinet?
No, I entered the band playing tenor saxophone, you know. Yeah. Because, you know, "tenor part", you know, tenor solos, Hahahaha.
Say a little about the transition that you made from the clarinet to the saxophone.
Ohh, there's no difference only...

the clarinet...it's the same fingering...oh, there's the embouchure and then the clarinet's got holes and the saxophone's got pads, so the saxophone's easier to play than the clarinet, 'cause you have to be precise in putting your fingertips over these holes so they will cover, so that you can make a sound.
Yes, but I'm thinking of your decision to change from one to the other.

Well, I liked the saxophone sound; it sounds like the human voice, you know. And everybody seemed to be fond of the tenor saxophone, you know what I mean. And I liked it myself; I didn't do it because I heard the public liked it. I liked it myself. I could have played alto, I mean, but I liked the tenor, you know. Yeah.
So do you remember the first time you went and actually played a gig with this group? And what it was called then?
Oh, Sy Jenkins and his Orchestra. Sure, I remember that. It was at the um...it was a high school dance, Central High School...now it comes to me...Central High School. We played a high
school dance and we had our music and we rehearsed and rehearsed. We rehearsed every day...and it was a high school dance. I think we got fifty cents, hahahaha.
Fifty cents apiece?
Yeahhehe.
What music did you play? You said you bought the standard...

Yeah, well we played the Glenn Miller Book, we played the Count Basie Book, the Jimmy Lunceford Book at that time, Casa Loma Band, the Jimmy Dorsey Band, the Tommy Dorsey Book, you know, so we had it made, you know. Everybody could read, you know.
Do you remember some of the first pieces you had a solo on, a tenor solo?
Well, let's see...oh boy, let me think now...
That's all right, we'll just shut this machine off for a minute...
So the first pieces you had solos on, you were saying one was...was it 'Marie'?

Marie. That was Bud Freeman's solo with Tommy Dorsey's band; that was a famous solo, And then of course I did all of the Basie solos. I did Herschel's . I did Lester's solos. And the Duke Ellington things; I did Ben Webster's solos. So, I was home free, shoot. It was great to have that music in those days, so the guys could...'cause in those days all the musicians all over the country, they knew every musician in every big band; they knew what part they played; when they played a solo, they knew what their sound was. And the singers, they knew them too and it was just marvelous, you know. From the bass, piano, guitar, trumpets, saxophones, singers...everybody knew everything. It was nice.
So did you finish high school?
Yeah, I finished. Yeah.
So were you in the band for those three years?
Yeah. You know I got heavier and heavier (into it) and I worked harder and harder, and I got pretty good. So my father wanted me to go to college right after that, but I was doin' pretty good
I thought I could go out in the world, you know, which he agreed to go try it, you know.

Let's spend some time with these three years when you were in high school playing high school dates. What kind of things do you remember about that period? What kind of development took place? You said things got a little heavier.

Well, even way back then I realized that I wanted to have a sound, because...listening to Herschel, listening to Ben and I heard some things by Coleman Hawkins in a music store...and I wasn't aware of him, because I'd heard Chu Berry and I loved him. And I became involved in sound. Chu Berry and, of course, Lester and Herschel and...they were on the radio all the time and everybody in the country was playin' tenor saxophone. You either played like Herschel or you played like Chu Berry or Lester Young, in those days. And then there was Dick Wilson and then Ben Webster come in a little later, so anybody that played tenor saxophone, they were excited because tenor saxophone was popular and the people I was listening to were marvelous, you know. They had something. So I was busy. Hahahaha.
You mentioned hearing these musicians

Well, I had records, my father-- you know--then every once in a while he'd take me out. He took me to Flint (Michigan) one time to hear Cab (Calloway) in person and I heard Hilton Jefferson...there was all the other guys in the band, but I was saxophone conscious. So, I'll never forget this, there was a dance in Flint and my father took me over there and there was Cab's band and there was Chu Berry, one of my idols, and there was Hilton Jefferson. So they played 'Body and Soul' and Hilton Jefferson got up and played so gorgeous...I thought Chu was going to take the solo, but Hilton Jefferson took the solo and--I'm tellin' ya--the guys in the band applauded, so people in the audience applauded. It was just wonderful and I was so glad to meet Hilton Jefferson and make some records with him, later on. He was so...not only was he a great saxophonist, but he was a gentleman, you know, a nice person.
So this trip to Flint to see Cab's band...
That was with my father, he did that for me.
...was that the first time that you had really seen one of your heroes?
Yeah. Yeah, in person. Hahahaha.
What else do you remember about that particular show?

Well, I know Cab was out in front; he was singin' and doin' his thing, but I listened for the precision and the rhythm was beautiful, but I had my eye on Chu and then, after I heard Jeff, then I had my eye on him. But that was the highlight of that evening for me, 'cause my father knew I loved Chu Berry, see?
So just you and your father went?
Well, there was some other people, I don't remember, you know. I think it was a couple of other people went with us, yeah.
Did anyone that you went with and anyone that you knew then know any of the people personally, in the band?
Oh no, no, no, no.
So it was just a matter of going in and...
Yeah.
...you never had a chance to meet any of them?
No, no.
Do you remember any other live performances that you went to of any of the other people whose sound you liked?

Oh. Oh. Oh, I liked Roy (Eldridge). He came to Round Lake in Lansing and I rode my bicycle out there; it was three miles out, but I'll never forget this. This was in 1937, I think, and so...I couldn't get in, so I was lookin' through the...they had these bars up to the windows...he saw me lookin' in, so he says "Come on kid," and I come in and that was a great night. Roy was blowin' and he had Franz Jackson in the band and...let's see who else did he have? I think it was Zutty (Singleton) and I thought that was the nicest thing. I sat right on the side of the bandstand and they just blowed and blowed and

Roy sounded so wonderful, I never forgot that. I told him about it many years later. Yeah, that was a tremendous experience. Haha. I was into it by then. Ha ha. Yeah. But he was so nice to me, yes he was.
So your band in high school played around different jobs. High school dances and...

High school dances and, after we got popular, we'd do things in the community, you know, like a community dance, you know. When people want to have a dance and then once in a while we'd play a couple of clubs, you know, they'd want us, you know. We were pretty good. Yeah.
You got 50 cents for your first job, do you remember how much you got after that? How did things go?
Well, things fluctuated, might be 50 cents, then it might be a dollar and a half and when we got two dollars it was wonderful.
So you played these jobs on the weekend...
Yeah.
...then, at the end of high school, what kind of decision did you have? I mean what things did you think of doing and what were other things that were possible for you?

Well I found out from playing around and then, when we were in school, we'd go to these various cities and play and I heard other musicians and I felt that, uh...I discussed this with my father, I see he wanted me to go on to college. I said, "Well look, I think I want to go on out here," you know, and we discussed it and my first little jobs out of town were all right, people liked me and so it gave me encouragement to carry on. And so, my first job, after we discussed it--he said, "Allright son, go ahead,"--was in Saginaw, Michigan, and I was working with Kenny Anderson and he was a very brilliant person...
Now this is a change then from the person that was the head of the band that you had in high school? This was Kenny Anderson?
Yeah, well, this was my first job out of the city. Yeah.
I'm interested in how that job came
up; who knew you from the early band...?

When I look back, I don't know how this happened...Oh, oh yes I do know how it happened. I met...after I got started playin' pretty good... I met Thad Jones and Hank Jones in Pontiac which was 30 or 35 miles from my home. Goofus Carnell...now it all comes back to me...Goofus Carnell, he took us to... oh, we did some things with Goofus Carnell and he come to Lansing, Michigan, and he had heard about us from somewhere and he said, "Let's do something." So we went up to, one summer, we went up to Idlewilde. We did a whole summer up there and Chauncy Donaldson, Kansas City, he was in charge of the band and Goofus-- I look back on him and he played fair trumpet--but he looked like...he had a funny look about him, that's why everybody called him Goofus, Carnell, he looked Goofus, ya dig. Hahahaha. Well he was a pretty smart businessman. So the deal went down. He got us together, then we...Thad and Hank and then this Howard Brockington from my hometown was playin' trumpet.
Were Thad and Hank in the same band?
Yeah. Yeah. So we did the

Sunshine Gardens, we done the Sunshine Gardens in Saginaw, but what I'm tryin' to say is that when I was there I stayed in Sonny Stitt 's home. His mother was an ex-chorus girl and he was in high school and when he got out from school he'd come by and we'd practice and I stayed at his house all the time we was at the Sunshine Gardens in Saginaw.
How did you meet Sonny Stitt?

Well I don't know. They came by the club and I didn't have no place to stay and so he say, 'Come and stay at my house.' You know he was a very forward person, you know, he wanted to learn. In fact, then he was thinkin' about Benny Carter, You know, he had his alto and he had started listening to Benny Carter. That was my first job out of town.
So did this become a regular job?
We stayed there all that summer and then I went to Flint, Michigan, with Jimmy Lucky. He had a little six-piece band and Bernie Peacock was in the band and we did Grand Rapids and we did Flint.
Was there a change in material from...

Well, I became more aware of the instrument by listening to these people I mentioned before. I became more studious and more concerned with tone and technique and all these various things because all these people I listened to, that's what they had, you know what I mean. So you try to perfect yourself, yeah.
You mentioned some of the early solos that you did. By this time what kinds of solos were you really working on? What were your specialties?

Well, my main solo was Coleman Hawkins's "Body and Soul", which I knew note for note. And then the Basie things and then I began to start learning other things, you know, like "Stardust" and things like that. But Coleman Hawkins's "Body and Soul" got me over and all the Lester and Herschel Evans solos got me over, you know. So in those days that's when people know that you were thinking the right way.
Yeah. You've mentioned Herschel Evans a number of times in the past to me. He died...did you ever meet him?

No. No, I never met him, he died very young. Yeah. He was a Coleman Hawkins disciple and, from what I understand, everybody just loved him, you know what I mean, because he had a certain style about him, not only playing, but as a person. Certain characteristics that everybody admired and obviously he was a hell of a guy, you know. Yeah.
So by this time you were playing Coleman Hawkins?

Yeah. Coleman Hawkins mainly, because I liked his tone, then I started listeing to--um-- well of course Herschel and Lester, you know, I could play them because their styles were such that you could copy them.
(--) So when did you first become aware of Lester?

Well with Basie! He and Herschel were together. You know what I mean. Herschel's tone was heavier and Lester's tone was light and so I knew right then that I was going to lean toward...try to perfect a deep, rich tone. I loved Lester, but I--you know-- I leaned toward the heavy sound, you know.

(At this point in the interview Marshall Fisher, a friend, stopped by to say hello to Mr. Nicholas. As Mr. Fisher is a person long familiar with the jazz scene, I turned the recorder on during their conversation. Part of this is transcribed below.)
You knew Speedy too probably?

Oh yeah, my wife and I both gave Speedy blood...no, gave Jimmy blood, you know what I mean, when he was ill there. But I knew Speedy well. Shoot. You know, go to her house, go to their house and they come to our house and have dinner. One of them type of things. You know. And he and Jimmy introduced me to Eubie Blake. He and Eubie was so tight. I went over to...it was in Brooklyn, on Hancock Street, so Jimmy says, "Come on, we're goin' to Eubie's house." So we go to Eubie's house and they're talking all this heavy, heavy...they go to the piano and they talk... then we say we'll leave the women there and we'll go on downtown. So we went on downtonw and Eubie signed his name, or sumpin, and Jimmy got a new piano and I say, "Oh oh, what's goin' on here?" So he invited us, my wife and I, back again. This next time, it was Thanksgivin' and his wife cooked this great big turkey.

So then Eubie took us back in the room and he says this is the recipe when I was workin' in those after-hours joints in Baltimore. Man I looked at this, looked like ice cream. So I say, "What you goin' to do here?" So he put one teaspoon down there and I put that in my mouth and I thought the top of my head was comin' off. Hahahaha. He laughed. But then he and Jimmy got together there man, oh, it was somthin'. And so I'll never forget Jimmy Jones, you know, and Ellis Larkin. Ellis Larkin and...he's so marvelous, you know. He was a child prodigy, you know, and I remember when he wrote all the music, he was the conductor of the band of the Martha Raye Show years ago. Well anyway, Ellis and I became friends and we became such friends that I could play anything, any show tunes, the verse, anything. He says, "Go ahead, Nick, just start it." And he had all the chords. And some of these jobs it ain't nothin' but 20 dollars a night. And I say, "Look, don't you want to come and pick you up?" He says, "Nope. Nick, I'll be there." And he was there. I don't know how he got there and some places in Astoria...believe me, listen to me...if I didn't have my car, some of these places, man...I don't know how he got there but he was there. And we had a good time. Yeah.
(Section deleted)
Wherever you all were...

Oh yeah, we were talkin' about piano players. Jimmy Jones. We were at Cafe Society with J.C. Heard's band and Al McKibbon and Joe Newman and before that was George Treadwell and when Sarah came in ...I became aware of her when I was in Earl Hines' Band, because they were excited about this young girl that won the award at the Apollo Theater, you know. Everybody was excited about her.
You were in Earl Hines' Band when she (Sarah Vaughan) started?

Yeah. So I began to listen to her, you know, because...then she came into Cafe Society and she was, you know, so wonderful. She didn't even know how great she was, really, you know. And she was so warm. I'll never forget, when I got the job she was down there workin'. I was with Claude Hopkins, so I came back on intermission 'cause Budd Johnson quit the job and he recommended me, so they had to hear me. So I had an hour and a half off for intermission, so I came so's J.C. could hear me, ya dig. And I think I played "How Deep is the Ocean" on Budd's horn--or maybe I had my own horn--but when I finished, she (Sarah Vaughan)

says to me, "Oh, what's your name?" I says, "Big Nick." She says, "That was so beautiful." And that's our first real communication and I never forgot that. And so, you know, she went on out into the world and George Treadwell became her manager and etcetera. And I'd go by to see her at the Paramount and I'd go by and say...but you know, it was a thing whereas, it was nuthin'. uhuh. I just wanted to see her and say, "hello." I look back on that now and that's what I wanted to do, because I was really fond of her, you know, 'cause of the way she treated me, you know what I mean?
That band, when she got on that band was an amazing band already!
Oh my God!
A frightening band. Bird and Diz in the same band.
Yeah. Well, I will say this for Billy Ekstine, he really, really tried to help Sarah. I mean from his heart and all the guys, and Diz and Bird, and all the guys, you know and Kenny Clark

you know he was married to Carmen McRae at the time, but everybody got together. They wanted to make it, you know what I mean. And she was just a regular, you know, so she had the talent and she come out of church in Jersey and a choir and she had all the equipment and the main thing is she knew the keyboard, and that's a tremendous help because you can check yourself out anytime, you don't have to depend on bringing somebody in to check you out, you know what I mean, rehearsal. You rehearse yourself. Hahahaha. That's where that's at.
(Section deleted)
When did it occur to you that it took a lot of air to make that big sound? 'cause you got an immense sound, you got what I'd call the old time tenor player's Big Sound, you know...

Well, I'll tell you, I was impressed with Chu, he had a fluid sound. I used to catch Cab Calloway from the Cotton Club, on the radio, and he had a fluid sound. Now I'm gonna tell you how this thing affected me. I says "Well!", 'cause nobody played no faster than Chu, you know, he was fast.

But he had a flow in his tone and sometimes he would actually be brilliant, you know, some of the things he did. But then I heard Ben Webster with Duke and I says, "Oh oh. This is something else here." He had such imbeccable taste and his choice of notes and the way he placed them and his sound was so big. Then, I used to go to this record store, they used to get tired of seeing me, I never bought nothin'. ... I heard Coleman Hawkins do "One Hour..." and then I heard some other things, but I says, "Now this tone is bigger than all the tones." And I said, "There's a sophistication and there's some classical training here that's missing from the other two men I've heard.

Then when Coleman Hawkins came back from Europe and he did "Body and Soul" and with that subdued...and so I said, "There's another dimension." But it was heavy and deep and that meant that you had to have control. So then I started learning my breathing exercises and I became aware of my health, really, 'cause I was an athelete. But I really became aware of my health, which you have to go through, then finally when I heard Ben Webster...Ben Webster came to Lansing, Michigan, with Duke Ellington's Band and I heard him. I went back-stage; he was very nice to me. I think this was in 1938. So then, in 1941, I went to Danville, Illinois, with
Raschell

Jimmy Rochelle. So we come to Chicago, on a holiday, and I caught Coleman in person for the first time at Dave's Cafe which was at 55th and Garfield. And I heard that sound. Now, what actually I heard was that every note that he played...they were all the same bigness, all the notes. I says, "Ohhhh, ohhhhh," because the other tenor players, they had certain notes that they petted and they became bigger, but all of his notes were big. And it was really somethin'. When they do the show he came out from the kitchen playin' his solo on "Body and Soul". I think he had an eight piece band but, Jesus Christ, his sound was bigger than the whole...than everbody put together. So naturally he heard me hollerin' and screamin'; he looked up there and then I came down, he was very nice to me and so he says, "Come on, let's go outside," So we went outside and they had a car agency next door and he was lookin' at the new car and he says, "How do you like that?" I says, "Coleman, that's beautiful." He says, "I think I'm gonna get that." And that made me aware of him more. So what he was tryin' to tell me was that he's used to the best. He told me right then, he's used to the best. And he says, "I think I'll buy this tomorrow." I wasn't aware of him at the time and his life-style. But, then, that impressed me, you know

what I mean, 'cause this is the way he lives, you see. So that was another lesson. So, after I heard him, I says, "Well, look, I'm gonna...", then I started listening to Lester for his rhythm and whatnot. But then I became more aware that Coleman was...and the way people loved him and the way they loved Ben Webster and I could see that this is the type of thing I wanted to do. Then I found out, even when I was at home, Coleman Hawkins had an article in some magazine, I don't know where my father found it, but the whole article was about Picasso (sic). I says, "Who's Picasso?", the painter, and he was talkin' like he'd like to do some things, unaccompanied, like Picasso does. Now I didn't understand that at that particular time, but I says, "My God, what is this here with this man here?" Hahahaha. I says, "Ain't nobody else talkin' like this. I might have to get a little heavier here." So then I finally got...when I come to New York, he was very nice to me and had me to the house and cooked spare ribs and black-eyed peas, and also Ben, nice, very nice. And then he showed me his mouthpieces, ya know, and you have to experiment and you're always tryin' and this 'n that and the other and then I got a deeper insight. It's a 24-hour deal. Sound is 24 hours, every day. See? That's all I needed to hear; I was hooked then

on sound, ya dig what I mean? So when I learned how to...I went into opera singers and I found out how they would breath so I became curious about...how Coleman... he also...oh, oh...I made a mistake there, I was thinkin' about Pablo Casals, not Pablo Picasso, he wanted to do some unaccompanied things like Pablo Casals...but...
Pablo Picasso did things un- accompanied too.
Oh yeah, heck yeah. Yeah, shoot.

You know I was thinking of something when you told the story about Coleman Looking at this automobile for sale in a car showroom. I remember Cedar Walton said the other day that he'd never known what a Mercedes Benz car was until he saw that you had one...when he first knew you.

Yeah, well, you know I've always wanted the best in life that I could, you know, because you know I learned from Coleman...because when you see Ben Webster, he was always sharp. They always had the best saxophones in the world and they always sounded so beautiful. So I patterned my life like that, I looked for...so I says, "This guy might like a Buick, but I
wanted a Mercedes because I rode in one one time and it was just like sitting in your livin' room." I says, "Look, that's what I want." Hahahaha.
I have two questions to ask you. One was, when did you first leave your home--you know--leave your father's home and go out and stay on the road or whatever.
I left in 1941...yeah...and I didn't come back. I didn't come back. No. I was gone then.
You were about 19 then?
Yeah.
So you got out of high school and you stayed there for another year?
No, right after high school I went on out there.
You graduated in June and...
Yeah, went on...gone...yeah.

I look back on that now...I look back why people hired me is because of my sound. It wasn't really fully developed, but they could see which way I was goin'. They could see and hear that I was tryin' to get a sound.
Who first hired you?
In the big time?
Yeah.

Well, Kelly Martin in Detroit at the Club Congo. I'll tell you what I did. We went there one time...my father took me to Detroit and we went to the theater and we saw Andy Kirk and that's when I first heard Bird and Jimmy Forrest was in the band and Andy Kirk...he's in the union now, he's an official in the union, but he was so...I eventually ended up playing with him, a few jobs...and my father says to me, "My God, Charlie Parker, he sounds like a machine." Haha. Dig? I mean...that's another aspect of sound. Because he come from Kansas City.
Well, now, your father got some ears then?

He had some big ears, baby, Yeah. He said he was blockin' hats in Times Square in 1919. He saved his money up and he went to the Metropolitan Opera to hear Caruso and, a standee,...he says "Nick, I stood up there for over two hours," and he says, "Caruso sound just like a machine." Haha. So I remember all these things. So that sound was instilled in me then. I wasn't even aware of that, see? It was in me. But then I went all through Caruso, I went through Berno Chaliapin, the Russian, for sound. Anybody that had a sound. Bessie Smith, Paul Robeson, Mahalia Jackson and Mabel Mercer and Billie Holiday.
Mabel Mercer. Mabel Mercer scared me to death.
Yeah. Well she's so gorgeous. When did you first hear her?
Very first and only time it was just about five - six years ago.
Where was it at?
It was at the Carlyle.
Yes Lord.
Woman could not sing a note, you know, couldn't sing a note and just bring you to tears in an instant man.
That's heart...make you cry, make you stand up, make you do anything.
Most amazing singer, I think, I've ever seen.
Boy oh boy oh boy.
Utterly amazing. Brought me, literally, to tears.

You see, up on 52nd Street I missed her because I was over on the other side of the street. She was up at Tony's and I wasn't aware of Tony's. I was young and I listened to all the saxophone players, you know, on this end. Tatum and everybody. If I'd have just had the presence of mind or if somebody would have said something to me, I could have walked up the street in 1946 and heard her then. So she told me Billie Holiday used to come up there and listen to her. I know that Billie got a lot of stuff from her, with that sophistication and she said the boss
had to come up and get mad (at Billie) and tell her to come back and do her job. Hahahaha. Yeah.
So this is what I got together. So I figured that I'd go along with them and put all them together and, consequently, maybe Nick will come out. You know. Yeah. Hahahaha. Come on out of there.
You say when you first went into the big time it was Kelly Martin's Band, that was the first...
Yeah, at the Club Congo, yeah.
I just wondered what made it "the big time". I mean everone knows what "the big time" is, but...
That's for Detroit. That was the biggest city I ever played in. It was the big time for me. Yeah.

Kelly Martin had...it was Slim Jones's Place...he was quite a fella, and the Norman Hotel was right up stairs and it was a place where all the nightclubs were at and it was a corner there and they called it "Paradise Valley".
Paradise Valley was the name of...

That's just what the entertainers and musicians called it, "Paradise Valley", Like what it meant was when everybody got off of work, they all congregated at that block and everybody, you know, talked their thing and whatnot and so forth and so on.

So Kelly Martin, it was a 12-piece band, and Al McKibbon was in the band and Kelly was the leader and we had chorus girls and they'd bring that new act in every week, you know, and it was quite an experience for me. Course I could read, but it was a big town and then I began to hear guys. There was a guy like Lorenzo Lawson, he was a top tenor player in Detroit, and Moon Mullins and Lamont...and so I was gettin' around a little bit then and there was a joint where we could go and jam and then when the guys would come in like Basie, I think I was in Kelly Martin's Band...I think we worked there six or seven months. But, anyway, the guys would come in town and I got a chance to hear Don Byas in Basie's band and different ones would come in and I was, you know, gettin' to hear people, you know what I mean. It was a tremendous experience, but one of the biggest experiences was one night we was all in "Paradise Valley". We'd all got off from work and it was silence, I didn't hear a pin drop, but i heard these taps...he didn't even have on

taps, he had on his shoes. And it...ohhh...I'd never heard anything like that before in my life, getting into sound. Everybody had their head down and this man was tap dancin' on the sidewalk, up side the walls, over the fire hydrants and whatnot. I say, "Who in the world is this?" They said, "This is Baby Lawrence." I says, "My God!" Can you imagine a couple hundred people congregated in a corner and they ain't nobody sayin' nuthin' and listenin' to Baby Lawrence dance. Ohhhh!

So that was another aspect of sound. Now I start thinkin', you know. And then, another time, there was Billy Holiday. I'll never forget, I was at the Paradise, so Billy Strayhorn says, "Nick, I got a ticket for you and I want you to come to this concert." I says, "Look, ya know I'm workin' here and whatnot and they mad if I turn around." You know, they want to make this money, 'cause we was doin' very well. So I just said, "O.K." So, let me tell you what happened, man. So I got there, so that meant I had to be at my job later on, but I didn't even care, 'cause Billy Strayhorn say, "You gotta go." 'Cause he lived right up the street from the Paradise and he used to bring all his friends from all over the world into the Paradise to see me.
That's jumpin' ahead though...
Yeah, well, yeah, yeah. Wait a minute now you made me lose my point there.
Strayhorn and watchin' Lady Day,

Yeah. Oh yeah, yeah. So I went to the concert and...I tell you what happened. Duke Ellington's Band...Charlie Parker and strings, Stan Getz and Billie Holiday closed the show. So I sit up there and listened to all this wonderful music and, when they finished, Billie Holiday got up there and started singin', it was like you had never heard anything all night. I says, 'My God!' So, hahaha, I'm tellin' ya, everybody was speechless, I'm tellin' ya. She just took out everything. You forgot anything that happened before; when she got through it was all over. I'm tellin' ya. And everybody knew it too. And I'm young and I really knew it, you know. Shoot. And the old timers that knew her, shoot, they weren't even worried about it, but it was a shock to me. A sound. So all these things come together. That's what helped me, you know, try to get this sound that I'm tryin' to get, you know, but it's not perfect and I work on it all the time, you know. Yeah.
Yeah, I want to bear down and get some
details about the period of time when you entered the "big time" with Kelly Martin and what you were doing just before that and how that job came about.

Well, what had happened, my father--like I said before--we went to Detroit to visit and we saw Andy Kirk and I first heard Charlie Parker and Jimmy Forrest. But my father, unbeknownst to me, he knew about the Club Congo and I think they were rehearsing that day and we went by there and he got Kelly Martin to the side... and Kelly Martin didn't tell me this till years later. He says, "My son is good, please hire my son, if you want him to play tenor or baritone, I'll get him a baritone." And I didn't know that until later. But when I first came to Detroit I worked in a place called Tom's Cabin with Tweed Beard, if I can remember correctly. And I had left Jimmy Lucky's band and I heard about this job. That's right, Tweed Beard brought me to Detroit and I worked at Tom's Cabin with him and then I worked at Cozy Corner with him and then Kelly Martin found out I was in town and then he hired me, you know what I mean. That's how that came about. He didn't tell me till years later that when my father and I visited Detroit, that my father got him to the
side and said, "Please hire my son." He told me that years later. I say, "Well, I'll be dawgone;" he says, "Yeah, your father told me." Hahahaha.
So do you remember, when you got hired with Kelly Martin's band, the procedure...did he come and hear you, did you go and blow some for him?

Well, no, I think he...word got around that I was in town and then he approached me. Yeah. And that's how that happened. Somebody was leavin' town; I forget the tenor player's name. Anyway, he left and there was a spot for me and it was wonderful because it was the first chance to play shows and see big time entertainers and people from all over the country and playing that beautiful music and the rehearsals and the whole thing. It was exciting for me. Yeah.
Who else was in that band at the time?
Well, there was a guy named Rev on piano. He was the arranger. And, of course, Al McKibbon...I don't remember the other guys names. I remember Al McKibbon was on bass and

Kelly Martin on drums, Rev was on piano and there was a trumpet player named Youngblood who was very promising. All I know is his name was Youngblood. But the other fellows, I can't remember who they were.
How large a group was it?
I think about seven pieces. We played a show and then after the show we played for dancin' and later on in the night we'd get a chance to play some of our charts and blow some, you know, yeah.
Now this was all at the Club Congo?

Yeah. I was there for quite a while. And that's when, you know, I started getting around and getting to be known and meeting other musicians and that's how I went with Earl Hines, by being in the Club Congo.
I see. Just stick for a minute with when you were still with Kelly Martin. You were living in Detroit at that time?
Yeah. I had a room right

across the street. And...I think it was the Carlton Hotel and there was plenty of places to eat right in there and the musicians were there all the time and the different bands were comin' in. I think the Alabama State Collegians with the Trenier twins were workin' up the street and that's when I met Matthew Gee and we used to practice. And I met...let's see who else did I meet? ...who else was in that band? Oh...we used to call him "The Saint", Austin, Johnny Austin. He played tenor, from Houston, Texas. We became quite friendly. But it was a nice time and it was a nice area. You know, when you're young and the stimulus was there and at that time Illinois Jacquet had made "Flying Home" with Lionel Hampton, which was a big hit at that time...
So what year was this?
This was around '41. And everything was, you know, it was a new thing. There was a new change because they'd heard about Dizzy. And it was a nice time to be comin' up in. Yeah.
So the show itself. What was the show like? You know, from begining to end.

Oh, we'd play opening number and then the chorus girls would come out and then they would have maybe a dance team or they may have a woman singing first and then they'd have a dance team and then the singing star, you know what I mean. I'll never forget the first time I ever saw Nina Mae McKinney. Of course, you know, she had a tremendous reputation and I had a chance to...that's big time you know...and I was really impressed, she had so much class, you know. And I found out later that she made a lot of movies and she was, you know, out in show business a long time.
She sang there at the Club Congo as part of the same show?
Yeah. Well then the next week they'd have somebody else. Every week was a different star, you know.
But Kelly was the house band there?
Yeah. He was the band leader and that was tremendous for me. I'll never forget that's the first time I got a

suit made. I always wanted a pin stripe suit and I had that thing made and this fellow, he staid in the hotel, he had his tailor shop upstairs. He made the suit a little too small but I loved it anyway and somebody stole it. I'll tell you I was really sick about that. Brown pin stripe, yeah me.

But that's where Benny Harris heard me, you know, when Earl Hines came to town and he came in the club and he immediately told Budd Johnson and Scoops Carey and that's how I was hired. Benny Harris, the trumpet player. Yeah. He passed on. But he was playin' like Dizzy then. You know he was...he really had the feeling of Dizzy and everybody was crazy about him in the band. In fact, everybody was crazy about Little Benny; we called him "Little Benny". And he got me in the band because I had a tone. I wasn't a great soloist, but I could read and I had a tone. And that's how that started. Then when I got in there, boy, it was really something, because Earl Hines's music was very, very, very difficult. And especially for the reed section.
Was he just passing through town then?
I don't know. I think they
were playin' a dance and they were around there for two or three days and I think they had a dance and then they laid over a couple of days.
Who did you replace in this band?
I'm tryin' to think who I replaced...umum. I can't think of that fella's name.
Before we leave Detroit, I'm just curious...places to hang out at the time. Were there other clubs that you went to?

Yeah. There was the Three Sixes and there was a late club up the street, I forget the name of that...where we could go jam and, oh let's see...oh there were several places there where you could go hear other musicians play so it was a nice atmosphere. Of course the Club Congo was it and then the Three Sixes. They had shows up there and then down the street there was a place called the El Zino and they would bring in jazz musicians. Yeah, El Zino, yeah...umhum.
So were you there for a full year?
I think I was there for about a year and a half. Yeah. That was good for me.
And then you went straight from that band, Kelly Martin's Band, straight to Earl Hines' Band?
Yeah.
And he was on a tour around the country was it?

Yeah. And it was quite a thing. And Billy Eckstine was the star and they had Shorty McConnell and Benny Green and Scoops Carey and John Williams, who was Mary Lou Williams' husband, at the time, on baritone, and of course Bud Johnson and myself and, let's see, Shadow Wilson was the drummer and I forget the bass player's name. He was a tall fellow, used to be with Louis Jordan for a long time. It was a good band. It was exciting for me. And of course Earl Hines's book
was an outstanding book and he had recordings out there. Earl was a marvelous showman and a great pianist and I was excited.
So do you remember the stops on the tour? As soon as you got on, do you remember what happened then?

I don't remember just what the first job was. But I remember one job. I know we played Cleveland, I think we went to Cleveland, then we went into St. Louis and then we went part way through the South, as I remember. We did some southern states.

I'll never forget we went into a place, it was Earl Hines and Billy Eckstine and myself and we went into the pool rooms. So Earl and Billy wanted to shoot some pool and there was this wise guy sittin' down in there and he says...they knew we were in town, you know, these guys sittin' around the pool room... and so he says, 'I bet you can't make that eight ball in the side pocket for five dollars.' So Billy, you know he had like a temper, he was..Billy had kind of a temper, you know what I mean. So he says, 'Sure, I'll betcha...', you know. So Billy shot the eight

ball and it went in the side pocket, so he says, "All right, pay me." He says, "No man," he says, "I bet you that you couldn't make, I mean physically make, an eight ball in the side pocket." Oh, that really teed him off and I'm tellin' ya we almost didn't get out of town. I think this was in Mississippi somewhere. Hahahaha.
Now it was with Earl Hines that you first came to New York City, is that right?
Yes, uhhuh...
That was really part of the same tour was it?

Yeah. And at the time I'd been with the band for a little while and I got the feeling that I wanted to study some more because I was out there for a little while, now I could hear what the guys were doin' and I felt within myself that I really needed some more study. So I was jammin' with...up at the Minton's, you know, we always...if you're off...I think Earl Hines's Band... we were off for about two weeks and so I was around

there and so I'd go up to Minton's, there was nothing else to do, go up to Minton's and jam every night. And that's when Sabby Lewis heard me, you see what I mean. And so he said, "Would you like to go to Boston?" And I'd heard about Boston where there was some good places to study and I said, "Well listen, I got to make a change here." So I went on to Boston with him and it was a beautiful relationship, you know. At first we did the Zanzibar...

I don't want to get quite to Boston yet, given how important New York was to become to you, I think we should spend a little bit of time on when you first came to New York. That was really your first trip to New York, right?
Yeah. It was my first trip to New York and of course Minton's Playhouse was the place, you know what I mean. Everybody was there...
Do you remember the first day you came to the City...how you came and who you were with?
We came in on a bus and I went and stayed at that hotel right next to Minton's,

what is the name of that hotel? Anyway, all the musicians stayed there and anyway I went right into the hotel, then Minton's was right downstairs. And that was just right for me. Boy oh boy, I'd come downstairs every night and Lester Young would be blowin' and Harold ("Doc") West and, oh gee whiz, Don Byas and I got a chance to really hear all these wonderful people and see them in this New York setting, you know what I mean, and it was just wonderful. And of course Kenny Clarke and Monk and, let's see, Eddie Davis was around there at the time and then he eventually became house band there. And Teddy Hill, you know, used to have a band in the Savoy years ago and he had all those guys in there...Roy (Eldridge). Chu Berry and what not and he even took a band to Europe, Teddy Hill did. Yeah. So he was the owner of the place. He used to play saxophone. So it was the place to be, you know, because you got the owner was a musician, saxophone player, and it was a place for musicians and that was just like being in heaven, you know. I learned something new every night.
Did you play any dates with Earl Hines here in the city when you first came?
I think we did a couple

of things. I think they were dances, if I can remember. And, you know, it was during war time and there was transition and people would go in and out of different bands and nobody was really stable, you know what I mean. So, from what I understand, somebody was going in the service and whatnot and it was transition so I felt that it was time for me to...it was an opportunity for me to make a change, you know what I mean, because I could...after being in New York and hearing different guys and hearing what I needed to study. You know, I said here's an opportunity for me, so I took it, you know.
Now you mention the war was going on and we know that a lot of people ended up going in the service...I mean musicians...
That's right.
What about your own case?

Well, I went in the service but but you see I only have one eye and so they took me in, but then I applied for a special service, you know what I mean, because I'm a musician and I didn't have any other skills, other than music. So they said

"Well, what the heck, I mean, we're all filled up here, I mean, you'd be better off out, you know, in the world. I mean playin' in a band, you know, because you don't have any special skills or anything like that." So I was fortunate.
So you were actually inducted?

Yeah, but I didn't serve any time, I mean not really, because I was just sittin' there, you know, because I wanted special service...musicians, you know, I could be in the band and I could be of some service, you know what I mean, because I didn't have any mechanical skills, you know...and other skills like that. So that's what I was shooting for and they were all filled up so that let me out. So I only stayed in the service for about two or three months. I used to go in town, in San Antonio, and...
Oh. You were stationed in Texas?
Yeah, at San Antonio...what's that um...anyway, I was there and there was a place where I used to come in and jam in a local band, I
forget the name of it and at the time I was with Tiny Bradshaw at that time, when I went in the service.
I see. Well, you came to New York in '42?
Yeah. Around '42, yeah.
With Earl Hines and then...
I went with Tiny Bradshaw...
While you were here in New York?
Yeah...
That transition happened here in New York?
Yeah and then I went with Sabby Lewis; that's the way that happened, yeah.
Why don't you break that down just for a minute, those transitions, you know, when you left one and went to another. Who took your place,
and whose place you took and things like that.
Well...
'Cuz I guess, as you were saying, a lot of change was happening there. So some of those changes took place quite rapidly.

Well, let's see now...oh yeah ...I went with Tiny Bradshaw, wait a minute let me get this straight now...oh, I went with Tiny Bradshaw and that's when I stayed in the Rum Boogie for 33 weeks and that's when I got Sonny Stitt[s] out of the Alabama State Collegians Band and Lucky Thompson was in the band [and] I got Howard Brockington, he was in the band, [and] I got him with Tiny Bradshaw.
That's your old friend, Howard Brockington?

Yeah, from Lansing, Lansing, Michigan, and so I went on the road with him for a little while and then when I came back, then I went... that's what happened...that's when I went to Boston with Sabby Lewis. Yeah. Yeah.
Before we get too much further, I want to compare a few of these people, just as you dealt with them as leaders, these different leaders: Kelly Martin and Earl Hines and Tiny Bradshaw.
That's a good point.
Maybe go back and, say the transition from Kelly Martin to Earl Hines...You marked Kelly Martin as the first person you went into the big time with.

Yes. Well, Kelly Martin was a good band leader and he loved music, but he was a firm band leader. He kept everybody in line. Of course he didn't have any trouble out of me because it was all so exciting to me, you know what I mean, but he ran a nice tight ship. And then when I got with Earl Hines it was a different thing all together, you know, he was so flamboyant and so much charisma. I mean I don't think he even noticed I was there, really, you know what I mean, because he was a showman, see. But he didn't bother anyone either. That's when I really saw what it's
like being on the stage, you know, out into the lime-light, you know what I mean. And that was a revelation to me. It all didn't come to me at once, but, you know, I look back and it impressed me.
When you mentioned that Kelly Martin ran a tight ship, were there rules that you all had to observe?

Oh yeah. You had to be on time and you be neat and clean and play, you know, Play the right notes, you know what I mean, and be a professional. No foolin' around, you know what I mean. And that's the way it was. And that's the way he was able to keep that job, because Slim Jones, he had confidence in him and, you know, it was a steady job, it was the best job in Detroit.
What was that paying for you? What was the range?
Oh, I think it was around thirty dollars a week.
Thirty dollars a week and you were
End of the week, yeah.
Were you paid by Kelly Martin directly or were you...
I think, when I look back, Kelly Martin paid us. Yeah. I think it was thirty or forty dollars, which was good money for me. My God, I thought it was a fortune. Hahahaha.
What did you spend the money on?

The room and food. That's all. Reeds. Music, you know. I met, one day, I met Vido Musso. Benny Goodman was in town and...he was a nice fellow...and we was talkin' about mouthpieces and sound and whatnot and then, another day, at this music store, I met Roy Eldridge in there. Hehheh.
In Detroit?
Yeah, in the music store.
Now, just to follow through this a little bit, as far as comparing some of the leaders that you've mentioned so far. Tiny Bradshaw. What was he like?

Well, he was like a Lucky Millinder - Cab Calloway type. He didn't know any music, he was just a showman. And he had a person that was in charge of the band and he (Tiny) was out in front, you know what I mean, and I'll never forget Tiny--God rest his soul, he's gone now--but we did a tour in the South and I became aware of jealousy and envy and things. I wasn't even aware of this, but Lil Green was very popular in the South. People loved her, her recordings of "In the Dark" and "Why Don't You Do Right?" which Peggy Lee was doing with Benny Goodman and, you know, makin' a fortune. But she was well loved. I'm just sayin' I could see myself that Tiny was a little angry because this woman so popular. They loved her. And she was a very dark woman. Then I found out later she had a bald head and wore a wig. Hahahaha. But she was a sweet person. But Tiny would stay out there so long before he'd bring this woman on and people was startin' gettin' angry. Hahahaha. They
come to see her, they'd seen Tiny for years, you know. But other than that, Tiny, he was alright. He never said anything to nobody, he just wanted you to play, you know. Yeah.
You did go on one or more tours with him?

Well, I did a tour with him through the South and then, as I say, we had this steady job at the Rum Boogie. Now at the Rum Boogie I became a part of the show. I mean they had the chorus girls and Ziggy Johnson who'd staged this show, he staged all the shows. You know, they changed every three or four weeks, but he had his girls built around me doing a number and that's when Lionel Hampton wanted me but I was makin' more moeny with Tiny so I didn't leave. Arnett Cobb came in, they were workin' downtown at a theater and Joe Williams was with them at the time. And I wouldn't go and then...
You were doing well with Tiny and...
...and I was happy.
...you were part of some act?
That was extra work within the band, then I had to go back and sit in the band. But that was a special number for me to do. See what I mean?
What was the number, do you remember?

I don't remember. It was a lively tune and the girls would dance and I was blowin' and he had some steps for them and it was a hit. And that made me quite popular and I was happy there. You know bein' on the job for 33 weeks is a long time and in Chicago and then my mother was there and my father came to see me. My mother was livin' there. You see. So that made it nice, you know.
What were you being paid then? Do you remember, for those 33 weeks?
I think I was gettin' about 60 dollars a week, which was great money then. I

think my room was eight dollars a week. And they have these jitney cabs in Chicago. You can ride as long as you want to for a dime as long as you didn't turn the corner. So I lived at the Oakwood Manor Hotel, so we walk up this block and catch this jitney, shoot, for a dime we was home. And those blocks are long in Chicago. So I mean we had it made. It was great.
And then was it after the tour that you took through the South with Tiny Bradshaw that you ...where did that tour end up?
Back in New York. They all ended up back in New York. And then that's when Sabby Lewis came by Minton's ...right back at Minton's... and he heard me, he hired me.
You were right back living in the same hotel as when you first came. It was like the place to be.
Yeah. The name will come to me.
What street was it on?
(The Braddock)
118th Street. Right over Minton's Playhouse.
Oh yeah, right over it. I've heard of that...
So Sabby Lewis came in and he heard me and he hired me. And that's how that happened.
What kind of a thing did he have going on?

Well he was an arranger and he was doin' things that the public liked. And he would buy music. He had Tadd Dameron write some things for him. He had a white fella...I understand he's a professor at some college in Brooklyn. His name was Jerry Hefron and he did a lot of the arranging. He had a good book, you know. When we were in New York at the Zanzibar, he had Freddy Webster in the band, Idrees Sulieman and George James...he used to be with Louis Armstrong years ago. We broadcast three times a night and that's when Leonard Feather heard me and that's when I started gettin' a little recognition, yeah.
So the work at the club Zanzibar was when you first went with Sabby Lewis?
Yeah...
And before you left for Boston? So about how long do you think that was that you were with him here in New York?

Oh, I don't know. I think we did about 16 weeks, I think. Yeah. And that was a great experience because I played Ethel Waters' act and I think we...I don't know if it was Broadway, it was a different situation and Joe Howard owned the place and it was really the big time. And I got to meet her pianist, Reginald Bean, who was a very gifted, gifted, gifted pianist and he was her accompaniest and we became quite friendly. I understand he works for ASCAP now. And Don Redman had the intermission band. Yeah. And he had Foots Thomas and his brother ...the other Thomas. And he had two tenors and I think it was Doc Cheatham playin' trumpet. He had a good band. Then this Latin flute player, I can't think of his name.* He came in with his intermission band, you know, playin' that Latin music, you know.
*possibly Alberto Socarras.
Then Dizzy would come by all the time and then...on my intermission I could run over to 52nd Street and hear everybody, then run back and hit the next show. It was exciting.
Do you remember when you first became aware of Latin music?..Latin jazz or Latin-influenced jazz?

Well, when I came to New York. Yeah. Well Dizzy was leaning that way when he did "Pickin' Some Cabbage" with Cab. That had kind of a Latin flavor, but I didn't really...because when I came to New York, you know what I mean, there was all these Latin bands and what not and all these people around here. A lot of the places--most of the places...the intermission band was a Latin band. Even then, 'cause people were doin' the Cha-Cha, you know what I mean, and the Meringué and people were doin' these dances then. And so that's what that was. And so I became aware of it. And I think Sabby got a couple of arrangements that had a Latin flavor, you know, and gradually I began to become aware of Latin music, you know. Yeah.
So you say it was with Sabby Lewis that you went to Boston. Did he have a regular stand there at some club?

Yeah. Sabby was like the Boston favorite. They loved Sabby in Boston and he had a place called the Savoy. It was like home, you see what I mean? When we went in there we was back home and then when he went up there he knew what to play for those people up there, you see. I remember we had one arrangement of "How About that...some band, That Mess" I can't remember the name of the band that made that popular and then he did the things that the people liked up there. Then we had all kind of arrangements and then I wrote some things.
Was this the first time that you'd written something that was used?...material that was used?
Oh, let's see...I think so, yeah. Well, 'cause I was goin' to school and I was experimenting, you know.
Let's get into that. You went to
Boston and I guess you were aware of the schools there, but did you have the intention...

Oh yeah, that's why I went, 'cause I wanted to study and Sabby told me he had a steady job and I said to myself, "Well, this is a chance to get to some things that I wanted to get to, like theory and harmony and sight singing," and so I got into that. And then I met Andy Jacobson and I took some lessons from him. He was a first tenor saxophone soloist that I can remember. He was a tenor saxophone soloist with Sousa's band and that, you know, and I said, "My goodness." And so I got to meet the man and I took some lessons from him, we became quite friendly. He was a nice man. And after that I started teaching his son jazz, 'cause I opened up a studio over the Savoy and I had students, you know.
Did you live there as well?
No, I had an apartment. Yeah. That's where I met my wife. It was a great experience for me. And a lot of things I wanted to get to, I was able to get to because I had a
job and I was going to school and then I had a little studio and then I got married and I was makin' some nice money. I think I was makin' a hundred-and-fifty then. That was good money.
For sure...so how many nights a week was the Savoy job?
Six nights. Yeah.
What school was it you went to?
Boston Conservatory of Music.
And how often did you do that? How many classes did you take?
I took a class every day for about six months. Yeah, I hung on in there. Hahahaha.
It was while you were taking the classes and while you were playing at the Savoy that you wrote your first arrangements?

Yeah. Well, at the time, you know, I did some things at...it was '45 and '46, they lifted the record ban and Dizzy and Bird had did some things and I wrote some things out that Denzil Best done, that I learned in New York. Then I did some of those Dizzy things for the band, Dizzy and Bird, and that's how I started to write a little bit.
What were some of the tunes (arrange-- ments) that you wrote then?
I think I wrote out "Sho' Enuf" and I think I did "Oo Bop Sha Bam"; I think I did "Salt Peanuts", you know, yeah.
[sho' nuff]
Did you write any original pieces?

No, at that time, I don't think I did, because I was all involved with the new sound and what not and, you know, they had so many arrangers in there, great arrangers, that what I contributed was the new thing, you know like Bird and Dizzy, you know. Because they had the guys that could write like this Jerry Hefron and Sabby wrote and then Al Hays, he used to be with Lionel Hampton, his trombone player, a fine arranger. He came into
the band for a while and he did some things. Music was comin' in all the time and I contributed my little thing, you know what I mean.
So how long did that job last at the Savoy?

Let's see that job must have lasted about a couple years. Yeah. And I decided I would come on back to New York, you know. I was married and my wife and I had a little money and we went and staid at her aunt's house in New York and that's how I got into New York.
Do you remember anything about the decision to move? I guess you were fairly settled by then...I mean...

Well, I felt that I'd accomplished what I wanted to accomplish in Boston and it was time to get back to New York to get the stimulus, you know. Headquarters. I'll never forget. I talked it over with my wife. I says, 'I'm gonna take fifty dollars and go into New York and see what's going on and what not.' And I felt that I could come
back and, you know, make it, you know. So I convinced my wife and we came back and stayed with her aunt for a while and then we...
Where was that?
That was up in Harlem; I think it was 142nd Street. And then we staid in another place and then after I got squared away I bought a house, you know.
Well, when you came back to New York, what was your first job?

It was with Scott...I forget his first name. He had one leg...Oh what's his name, Scott. Isn't that a shame I don't remember his name. He was a tenor player, clarinet player. And my first job was with him and I'll never forget John Hardy and he were friends and John Hardy came by and played and he was still in his army uniform and that's when I first met John Hardy from Texas, a very fine tenor player. And then, let's see, of course I was jammin', 'cause I had to wait out the six-month period, before you could take a steady
Cecil

job in New York City...that union thing. But we had a little money. And so I waited that out and then, you know, I went into the Zanzibar, a new Zanzibar, it was across the street from the old Zanzibar, with Claude Hopkins and George James who used to be with Louis Armstrong in 1928, a very fine lead alto player. He got me the job and that's when I got to play for Bill Robinson and so many people and that was Nat King Cole's first New York engagement with his trio.
Was it with the Claude Hopkins... I mean was he billed with them?

No, he had a trio. He was a star. He was on stage. That was a great experience, being with Claude Hopkins. You know I've seen him several times years later. I even got J.J. Johnson to do I think it was a couple of things for the band. Claude Hopkins bought music all the time. Yeah, sure. You know he played fine piano, you know. Yeah.
So what year have we gotten to now, you've come back from Boston...
We're in '45 now, gettin' ready to go into '46.
(Pause)

You know when we spoke earlier I asked you who were some of the earliest influences that you had and you mentioned people like Chu Berry and Herschel Evans and I wonder now, some years have gone by and you've established yourself in the big time, playin' with the big bands and I wonder at this point, say in the middle '40's, who you were most listening to, whose sound was most attractive to you?

Well Coleman Hawkins, mainly, because he seemed to have everything.
