All of his notes were clear and beautiful and he had an evenness about his horn and then his brain, he seemed to have such a deep knowledge of sound and chord structure and he just seemed to have everything. And he was actually cultural in his sound. And later on I found out that, you know, he played piano and played cello. And when I went to his home several times, then I realized that he had all the operas and all the scores and he played beautiful piano, as I said before, and this was the man, you know. And I liked Don Byas, because he was smooth; he had a

tremendous technique and he had a nice understanding of musical structure. And he had good time and he was just absolutely great. Now Ben Webster, his playing was...he had such a big gorgeous sound and he had such marvelous taste. His choice of notes was so attractive. And these three people I watched all the time.
I wonder, you knew Coleman Hawkins when he was playin' regularly on 52nd Street.

Yes, well everybody knew he was my idol and I dressed like him, I played like him and I had a moustache like him. And, you know, I was there all the time. So one night he said, "I think I'll play 'Body and Soul' in E natural." So I says, "O.K.". And we played it and he laughed and he said, after that, that I was his boy, you know what I mean. Every time I come in there, if he wanted to go somewhere he say, "Go on up there, 'cause they think you're me anyway." He'd go off and stay an hour and a half and, oh, I was in heaven. And they had Denzil Best on drums, Al McKibbon on bass and Monk on piano. And then I noticed things about Coleman, you know. All of

his shoes were hand made and all of his suits were made, his shirts were made. And he was just a classy person, yeah. And he always had a new car every year and he always had fresh horns. He only kept a horn about six or eight months, then he'd get a new one. So I says, "Why you do that?" He says, "Well, son, you gotta always keep your horn fresh." And I never forgot that.
Did you have a car, yourself, by this time?

No, I didn't have a car then. I didn't get a car until 1954. I rode the subways and buses all those years. Yeah. From Long Island, you know, 1946 when I bought my house, I caught the bus and rode the subway and I did it all those years.
O.K. Getting back for a minute to the sequence of bands you were in. You mentioned Claude Hopkins and your time with him. Now, when you left Claude Hopkins, who did you go with after that?
Well, I went with J.C.

What happened...you know after the show you had about an hour and a half break and so I went down to Cafe Society. I took a cab and went down there, because Sarah Vaughan was workin' there and J.C. Heard band was there and he had George Treadwell was in the band and Dicky Harris and Jimmy Jones was playin' piano and I loved him so and, of course, J.C. Heard and Al McKibbon. So I went down and J.C. asked me to play one because Budd Johnson had quit the band. And I played "How Deep is the Ocean" and they liked it and so...and then Sarah Vaughan was there and she give me encouragement, she say "That sound so good." And that knocked me out. So then I went back up there (Zanzibar) and didn't say nothin' to nobody. Then I went on down with J.C. Heard. And that was really a fine job, 'cause J.C. Heard is so marvelous and he was so clean, you know. We rehearsed and Jimmy was writing things and that's when I started writing some things. I think my first music for the band was "Who's Sorry Now". And we were broadcasting three nights a week, I mean three times a night. And this was a place for the international set and you'd see Ingrid Bergman, Frank Capra, you might see anybody in there. Paul Robeson was in

there all the time. Canada Lee and all these people. It was just an international atmosphere. And it was beautiful. Leonard Feather was livin' upstairs and that's when I got, you know, to get to know him. And Mary Lou Williams used to come in and James P. Johnson was the intermission piano player. Then Josh White was the star sometimes.
Now, Josh White, I didn't realize that Josh White had played there.

Yeah. The folk singer. And Susan Reed, they liked her. She played lute or somethin' and she sang folk songs and it was just nice. It was just nice and that's when I bought my home, you know. Then all our people would come in, like Lester would come in and visit and Sid Catlett would come in and visit and Norman Granz and Illinois Jacquet came in a couple of times and jammed. It was just wonderful. There was good money; I think I was makin' over 200 dollars a week. Yeah. And that's what give me the idea to buy a home. So that's why I bought my home. Yeah.
(dulcimer)
So how long did you stay...
...with J.C.? Almost two years.
And that was right there at the Cafe Society?

Yeah. Well what happened there, we were doin' a benefit at the Apollo Theater and of course John Hammond had a lot to do with the Cafe Society, you know, he had Teddy Wilson and I mean he and Barney Josephson were friends, but there was a misunderstanding. We went up and did this benefit at the Apollo Theater for a "cause" and they didn't like that. That's the first time I saw the New York thing, you know, everybody was mad. Hahahaha.
Say some more about that.

Well everybody got mad and behind that we got eight weeks' notice. That's how we lost that job. Yeah. We weren't late. We weren't that late. We came back and finished out the night, but they didn't like that. And that's how we lost that job. Then we went to Washington

and then after that the band broke up. But that was a great band. We did some recordings behind Etta Jones at the time. I'll never forget, we did Loew's State Theater, which was a big barn down here. And Etta Jones, may God bless her, they liked us all, but it was a very cold theater, but they loved her. And that impressed me. Etta Jones. I understand she's doing pretty well now.
Yeah. I saw her just recently, a few weeks ago, at the St. Charles Auditorium.
And she's got some fella that plays nice tenor, Pierson or something?
Houston Person, from Newark.
Yeah and they're together all the time. I heard a recording that they did. It sounded good. She's really singin' her heart out, yes she is.
So that was the first time that you had heard her and met her was at this time at the Cafe Society, must have been--what--'47, somethin'

Yeah, '46, umhum. I don't know what happened there. How she got with the band, I don't remember. But I know we did Loew's State together and she broke it up. That was a cold house. That's when I began to realize that Broadway can be a cold place, 'cause our applause was very chilly. Hahahaha.
So you had this trouble with playing up at the Apollo Theater and being late or somethin' like that...

Yeah, comin' back to the job. Yeah and that was a real shock, you know, for all of us, because we were set there and then everybody was crazy about us, you know. So that just broke that up, you know. Yeah.
Then you say the band, as a band, went to Washington for a while...
Well we did a few things, but nothin' ever happened after that. It was a shame.

We were singin' in harmony and Jimmy Jones was writin' all of Duke's things. Yeah. He was a Duke Ellington man and he was writin' all those Duke things like "Check and Double-Check" and "The Girl of My Dreams Looks Like You" and all these pretty things, man. Oh my God, it was just marvelous. Yeah.
So who did you go with after J.C. Heard's band broke up?

Well, let's see, what did I do after that? Well that job actually broke my heart, it really did. I was a little lost there for a little while. And then I did four or five weeks with John Kirby at the Apollo Bar and Grill. Then I did the same job with Doug Bascomb.
Dud
The Apollo Bar and Grill, that was next to...
No, that was a block away from the Apollo Theater. And, what else did I do? Well, I worked around and gigged with different people, but then in 1948 Dizzy called me. You know, he sent
me a telegram and then I joined his band. Yeah.
Do you know how that came about?
Ike Quebec. He wanted Ike Quebec, but Ike didn't want to go with the band so he told him about me. So Dizzy sent me a telegram.
I see. Ike Quebec was a person that you'd known...

Oh yeah, shoot,yeah. Shoot, I'd knew him in Chicago when I was with Tiny Bradshaw. He was workin' down in the Loop someplace and...but Ike was always a nice, nice person. He played piano and was a great tenor player. And, main thing, he was a nice human being. And we became friends. Yeah.
So Dizzy sent you a telegram; where was he at that time?
Well he told me to meet him in Detroit. I don't know where they were out on the road, but I met the band in Detroit. Yeah. In a theater. And that's how I started with Dizzy.
Had you known Dizzy personally before?

Oh yeah, sure. Benny took me when I was with Earl Hines'...Benny took me to...I think we did...I think with Earl Hines we played the Theater and after the show Benny told me "Let's go. I want you to hear Dizzy." I say, "Yeah, he was with Cab" and he'd really impressed me that night. And he and Benny were friends, you know. And that's how that happened. Yeah.
Dizzy had such a reputation as a rascal when he was a member of like Cab's band, always cuttin' up. How was he as a leader at this time?

Well, he was disciplined. You know, he had a lot of experience. He came to New York in 1936, so he had that discipline, you know what I mean. In other words, "play correctly", you know what I mean, 'cause he come up under Benny Carter and Coleman Hawkins and all those guys and, you know, he was smart, you know what I mean. He knew that this was the way the shit had to be, because he come through the ranks, you know what I mean. And everybody re-

spected him for his musical knowledge and that foolin' around, that became just a part of an act. You know, after he had became more responsible and responsibility and etcetera, etcetera, that image of "Dizzy", you know, that just became part of an act. But, actually, as a business man he was on the ball.
So you started working there in Detroit, your first job with the Dizzy Gillespie Band.

Yeah! That was quite an experience because in the atmosphere...Louis (Armstrong) was there too. He was...just formed his new sextet with Jack Teagarden and Earl Hines and Arvell Shaw and I think it was Zutty (Singleton) on drums. And I worked steady, between Lynchburg and Charlottesville, for practically all the seventies. Yeah.

'72. Yeah. And this was, you know, a small community, but they had a nice club. The guy that owned the place was from Detroit and he was a big city man and he went down in there and he liked music. We made money for everybody we worked for, you know.
Something occurs to me here that

A lot of the things they were doin' I don't even know nuthin' about because...and then, there was really no stigma to it, but it was a little sad, you know. So you try to hang on as long as you can, you
know, before you have to make a decision like that, you know what I mean.
Did it ever seem to you at some point that...
Oh yeah, many times. (laughter) Yeah, there's been some rough weeks there.
So where was your wife in this, in terms of the...
Well she was workin' all the time, yeah.
Would she urge you at some points that you should take...
Yeah, she told me to go in the Post Office and get somethin' steady, you know.
I guess Charlie Mingus worked in
the Post Office at one time.

Oh, I know, J.J. Johnson was...I think he's still in the Post Office out on the coast. Sure. I know Roy Haynes became a whiskey salesman. You know, you try to think about different things. Try to survive, that's the whole thing. You see what I mean. Tryin' to make it, see. But I didn't do anything, say "I'm gonna try to make it some kinda way." Of course I was learning all the time, you know, about all facets of the business, you know what I mean. So all these things that you learn, you know, you put 'em in the bank and one day it will all come out, you see. But the lessons were hard. Yeah. (laughter) Yeah, they were hard Dale.
So, in Virginia you did eventually take a job as a musical consultant...
When I came to Charlottesville, yeah.

No, no. But what happened...I knew when I was doing these club date things that sometimes there'd be a lot of children there and the children always used to stand up and look at me. And they'd sit down and just look at me. And then when I get off they want to know my name and we'd shake hands and we'd get to have our little conversation. So, I say, "Well, doggone." Well, I didn't think any more about it. But, anyway, I got to Charlottesville and this particular person, he was a professor and his wife was an intermediate school teacher. And he used to just come into the place all the time and he said to me one night, "Nick, why don't you come over to my school and do something for my wife's class." So, I knew I liked children back in my heart, you know deep in my heart, but it just hadn't come out, you know. I mean the real meaning of it, you know. So I went over there and I said,

"oh, Ill do it for nuthin'," you know, "'cause you come in the club all the time." And he was makin' plenty of money and he was real nice, you know. So then I did another day and then I did so well, then the public school system, they approached me. And so I did that for two years, the children from kindergarten to 12. Of course the kindergarten children you have to be very visual in order to hold their attention. But I'd ask them what they want to be and then get them up to dance a little bit and sing a little song together and I'd play my horn and everybody had a good time, you know. So what I know in my heart is that it only takes one situation for a child to see or for somebody to say something and it'll give 'em a spark. It doesn't have to be a musician, but they could be whatever they want to be, 'cause I'd ask 'em whatever they want to be, just work hard and you'll make it. And this one wanted to be a veterinarian

and this one wanted to be a astronaut and this one and this one...whatever it is. And then I'd ask them to ask me a question and I told them the reality of life and what the real world is like and, you know, it seemed as though they wanted to hear that, you know. Then I realized that these children have got a little sub-culture, you know, and they'd get together and discuss what I did and this and that and the other and so it got to the point there where everywhere I would go in Charlottesville, if my head was down, they'd say, "Hey Big Nick," and they would say it with such affection and my head would be straightened up...(laughter) And then I did the private schools, too. And then I did...

So that's how that happened. It was very successful and I started with the history of the saxophone and the different styles, you know, starting with Coleman Hawkins, from 1921 and then came on up to John Coltrane, you know. And the college students they were crazy about Coltrane and

he wrote a tune for me called 'Big Nick' and that seemed to bring me out of the woodwork a little bit, because the college students they were very fond of John Coltrane and they wrote several books on his life and I was in the books. Now I won't pursue that statement, but you know what I mean. (laughter)

Now Hilton Jefferson had it, you know, I had the pleasure of playing with him. We did some record dates together. He had that all his life; he was totally dedicated. And, of course, Ellis Larkin. Related to this in some way, I wanted to know...the transition from your playing
in big bands to playing in smaller groups, some of the things that were involved there and some of the things you remember about that.

Well, in the big band it was like a family, 18 pieces. And then if you were a soloist, you know, you played the arrangements and when you come to your solo then you sit up and played your solo. But it was a confined thing, you see what I mean, like you might have two solos a night or you might have four solos a night, but the rest of the time you're just playin' parts, 'cause someone else is soloin' or you got a singer or whatever. But in a small group you have a chance to be more creative because you can play what you want to play. You can play as many choruses as you want to play. And you grow artistically, as an individual, you see what I mean. You have that freedom, you see what I mean. Now I loved the big band experience that I had 'cause it taught me a lot...the unity and togetherness of guys and playing together. But in a small group you have more freedom and you can explore and exper-

iment and it's just better for a soloist. Yes, umhum. That's why Coleman Hawkins, they come up in the big bands, and Dizzy and Bird was in a big band and Coltrane played in big bands and most of these guys that became soloists, eventually...Dexter was in a big band, Illinois Jacquet, Don Byas, Ben Webster. All these guys were in big bands, but eventually they felt that they could have more freedom by being with a small group, which proved to be true, you know. Yeah.

Well, there was another change that was taking place too and it gets to another point that I wanted to talk about and that is the thing of playing dance music, or at least music that people were dancing to, as opposed to the situation that often happened with smaller groups, and with the change in style generally, where it ceased to be dance music.
Well, dance bands, playing for dancing is an experience that you have to feel. Now you playing a dance, 18-piece band, and you got two or three hundred people on the floor, you got

to play music that they can dance to, so you have a rapport. Now these particular people that I mentioned, if they had a four piece job, I mean a rhythm section and a soloist, they could still play for dancin' because they had that experience of playin' in the big band. Now, the delicate fine line is between...if you're playing for a dance and you got a four piece band...is to play for dancing and to play for listening too. Now what's been happening here lately is people that are in this particular situation, they'll play for dancing for a while and they'll do a few things for people to just listen, you know what I mean. And then they go back to the dancing. And that's what you call experience, you see. Yeah. Now just listening is one thing, but playing for dancing is another thing. Now, if you have both of those experiences that's, you say, more of a feather in your cap. (laughter)
I wonder, looking back over the jobs that you've had, you've talked about in previous tapes, which of those were more or less exclusively dance oriented music and when did changes take place in that?

Well, the changes took place right after the war, you see, World War II. People wanted something different, so they were in a listening mood and that's how Dizzy and Bird and people like that were able to come to the fore. Because people were in a different mental frame of mind, they wanted to hear something new. And the war was over, and so that was a perfect time for this to come through, you see what I mean. People still went to dances and what not, like the Roseland's been there forever. You know, people have been dancin' all their life and they're dedicated to dancin'. You know, you go to Roseland and you got people 70 and 75 and 80, dance, because this is what they love, you know what I mean. So the band that's playin' at the Roseland, they know what they got to do, they got to play strictly dance music. Now if you were playing in a different type of place, where it's a listening audience, then you do this other thing, that people listen. It's all a matter of experience, that's what it is. You know, the older you get you have to have that experience. Now, if you're playing in a place where people

are listening, if a person has this expertise where they can make people happy if they're not dancing, as if they were dancing, and get that same feeling. Now that's an extra dimension and, in other words, all that people have to do is tap their feet and clap their hands and what not. But if you're a person that has that talent to be able to make people feel that double feeling, you know what I mean, now that's something extra. That's special, you know what I mean. Do you enjoy playing for dancing?

Sure, there's a certain stimulus there, you know, because my experience through the years. It does something to your horn, to see people dancing. It's a spiritual thing, you know. Now, if you haven't done it, you don't know what it is, so you don't never know what it is. But if you've been through it, then you know what that is. Yeah.

And the partiucular thing that you're looking for, you can't get it, then you try another mouthpiece, you see.

I have an Yeah. In reeds, you know, through the years Van Doren had the best reed, then we tried Vibrator, then there was a time when things went bad, during the war, we was usin' plastic reeds. And then I finally ended up with Rico Royal, because they seem to hold up and last longer. Yeah.

Number three. Yeah. That Rico Royal is a very strong reed, it holds up. Yeah. It's got a nice sound to it.

Well, saxophone player, trumpet player, they always have this problem with their teeth so I had some work done on my lower mouth and it cost me twelve hundred. But, you know, through the years your mouth, your gums and your bone structure...all that pressure through the years, you know, it wears away and the bone structure wears away and then your gums recede. O.K., now, coming along a little further, I wanted to be more clear than I am now about Timmy Rogers. It was with him that you worked with Buck Washington, right?
Yeah.
Say a little more about that if you would.

Well, Timmy was on stage when he was a child, with a thing called "Me and My Shadow". He was a child star and his tradition on stage goes way back. But he liked me because he could see that I had, you know, some potential to be on stage also. And he encouraged me. He was a friend and I learned a lot from him. And of course when we got our act together we played. And, incidentally, Linton Garner came in, Erroll Garner's brother. But this particular thing...we had two girls and Austin Powell, who had the "Cats and Fiddles", he wrote "I Miss You So", in fact "I Miss You So" is on the back of "Lush Life" of Nat King Cole's. Yeah. And Jumpin' George, he used to be with Arnett Cobb. He was a show drummer...
What was his name, Jumpin' George...?

I think his name was Jumpin' George Jones, I think his last name is. Anyway, we had an act and that opened up a new world to me, of the stage and stage business. And that gave me a new dimension, you know what I mean, 'cause the stage is very serious...a lot of people think...and of course Timmy was a comedian, but he sang and people thought that... you know people on stage...but it's very serious and dedicated worker...it opened up a new world for me. But Timmy Rogers encouraged me and so did Buck and Bubbles. He was my roommate and my car-mate when we go on the road. And he taught me a lot too. And then, of course, Austin Powell, you know. They were all stage people, you know. Yeah. We went to Atlantic City and did a whole summer and that almost killed me, because I had never...I had to open the show blowin' and singin'. We did three shows a night, seven nights a week and then on Saturday nights they did the breakfast shows...went into Sundays which made seven days. Then they'd bring these people in that had these parties on Sunday after-
noons. So we end up some weeks doin' nine days. I'd never been through nothin' like that before. But that was show business. (laughter)
O.K. I want to ask a little bit more about your recordings. Una Mae Carlisle. You recorded with her?
With Don Redman. Yeah.
Say something about that recording date, if you would.

Well, it was beautiful. Don Redman was so gifted, you know. Every note...I always said this about Don... all of his, if you're playin' harmony notes, all of his notes sounded good. And of course Una Mae was near the end of her career. I didn't know her but she had a tremendous sensitivity and she sounded good on the date and Hilton Jefferson and George Dorsey and, let's
see, who else was on that? I think Milt Hinton was on that and Buck Clayton and it was beautiful. We did two days. Yeah. It was just lovely.
Where was that recorded?
Columbia. Umhum. I had a couple of solos on that date.
One of the reasons I asked about that is that I don't believe that you noted that in the list that you made up for me to look up those old 78's.
Yeah. I forgot that one. I forgot that one. Yeah, well I was on that date; that was a very memorable date.
What was the very first time that you went into a recording studio?
Well, let's see, I can't even remember now. Let's see. It was
with J.C. Heard when we first went into a recording date. J.C. Heard, when we left Cafe Society.
That was after the Cafe Society job ended?

No, we were doing some dates when I was there. We did some things behind Etta Jones, for RCA Victor. Then I did some things with Trummy Young which John Levy did before he became George Shearing's manager and Jimmy Jones and Ray Nance. I don't know what ever happened to them. Bob Thiele produced that date. I don't know what ever happened to those records. I never heard anything about that. That was a great date. Jimmy Jones made the arrangements. Trummy sang and Ray Nance played. It was good. I would like to find those.
What year was that?
Oh, it was around '46, '47. Yeah.
'46 was the year you did "Open the Door Richard" with Dusty Fletcher.
Yeah. That was recorded ...we were in Cafe Society at the time I did all those things. Yeah. But that wasn't the first one I did. The first ones I did was with J.C. Heard on RCA Victor, you know.
Then you did "St. James' Infirmary" with Hot Lips Page, that was '47.
Yeah.
Could you say a little something about how that date was set up?

Well, "Lips" liked me and he said he wanted me, you know, to record with him. We rehearsed and we did it for Columbia and he recorded one of my tunes called "La Danse" and he let me play, you know, solos a and it was/beautiful, relaxed date, you know.
"Lips" was so wonderful, you know.
When did you first meet "Lips"?

I don't know. I met him around town. I don't know exactly what day it was, or what not, but--you know how musicians are--they had to change all the time and I met him somewhere, you know he let me play somewhere.
"La Danse" was the first of your own tunes that was recorded. Then "Deedle-ee Deedle-um". Did you ever record that yourself?

Yeah. I recorded that with Timmy Rogers. That was on RCA Victor and, of course, (Jon) Hendriks did it at the Newport Jazz Festival. Yeah, live. Yeah, Coleman Hawkins and Clark Terry, I forget who else was in the band behind it. But I couldn't make that job. It broke my heart, He wanted me to come out there and do it, you know, but he did a good
job.

They always want you to be on time, then you get there and you never knew what was going to happen. You wrote the music and you wonder, you know, if you would be able to play the music and then if you had a solo, naturally you were concerned about your solo. Well, the Manteca solo I enjoyed very much doing and then the things I did with Buck Clayton, Frankie Lane on Columbia. I liked those solos. And some solos I did with J.C. Heard on RCA Victor with Etta Jones, I liked some of those things and then those things I did with Trummy Young. Those records were lost; I don't know where they're at, but I liked what I did on those.
I remember when you were doing the radio interview with Phil Schaap on (W)KCR, you had some phone calls...some people called in... I remember Al Hibbler...

Oh yeah, Al Hibbler, my God I love him so. You know Al is a really dedicated singer and I know,..we were stayin' at the Braddock Hotel and we used to get up and I'd get my horn out and he'd try to make sounds, and he'd make sounds, and I'd make sounds and we used to have a good time. And then I'll never forget one time he asked George Shearing, he said, "Look George Shearing", 'cause Al Hibbler, when he had eyes (someone to accompany him), he'd go anywhere. Anywhere, he'd go anywhere. So he asked George Shearing one time, says, "Look George, let's hang out one time," and George say, "No, no, no." But Al Hibbler, I really appreciate him calling me and he's always been a real close friend throughout the years. May God bless him.
You stayed with him in a hotel in New York. That was...
The Braddock Hotel. When I was at the Zanzibar with Sabby Lewis.
You know, most musicians stayed there, That's right around the corner from the Apollo Theater ...right on that corner.

In the time that you had off from work, say in the early days, who would you make a point of going to see...you've said quite a bit about your heroes, Coleman Hawkins and whatever, but were there other people, perhaps lesser known people around at that time that you...

Well, let me think, that I really liked, let's see..I can't think right now, but there were some people. Oh, I liked to hear Budd Johnson play, you know, and I liked to hear Zoot Sims play and I liked to hear Gerry Mulligan. I liked the way he played. Maurice Mark, I liked the way he played. I liked Stan Getz, you know. He was playing very well at that time. I liked to listen to Red Norvo, you know.

From the periods of time that we've covered now, it seems as though your career was building well, and the Paradise was a good job, and after that things went down hill a bit. And, as you've already mentioned, that coincided with "Rock 'n Roll" coming on the scene.

Well, what actually happened was they started recording these groups, the Birds, the this , the that and the other, then they would have jazz musicians be the backup musicians. But then they decided they wanted the tenor to sound like a cow and sound like a hawg. In other words, prostitute yourself, you know, all the years that you've studied and tried to create a beautiful sound. They didn't want that; they wanted noise, you see what I mean. Then, come to find out, most of these groups, the kids didn't know anything about the idea of music and it was just terrible. And then when the kids, you know, you play this stuff, and they didn't know what they were doin'. They had no idea of harmonics, no musical background and they were rushed in there and we had

to cover for 'em, you know. It was so sad. Then when they got their own groups, they didn't need the jazz musicians, real professional musicians to back 'em up. Then they come in with their thing, which they only knew three or four chords and the main thing is that they were loud and that they were young and the industry concentrated on young people. And they actually created a monster, because these young kids, they didn't know anything about music, really. They didn't know anything about music, no. But there's nothing you can do about it, you see.
Now, did you ever have an opportunity, I mean was it ever offered to you to work with any of this kind of situation?

Yeah. I worked with some of the things, but my heart wasn't in it, you know what I mean, and I couldn't do exactly what they wanted me to do. And, you know, you're just prostituting yourself, you know. That's what you're doing. You were demeaning yourself. And it got to a point where it became
disgusting. Because the guys that did this to make a dollar, you know what I mean, they weren't being creative or anything and it was just a downer. Yeah, yeah.

Then, of course, jazz itself, when it became popular...it's phase of popularity in the '60's, it was quite a different style, for the most part, from that which you came up with. Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane in his later years...

Well, that's another thing in itself, you see. When Coltrane came out with his thing, people said his tone was terrible, but what they didn't realize is that John Coltrane was a student, a serious student of music, you know what I mean. And he eventually came on through there. But that period of creation was a very chaotic situation. The guys were trying to create something new and they got adverse publicity. And they got a "no, no" from the public and it was very sad and I
didn't want to be part of that, really. Of course all the guys...we were friends, you know. I knew what they were doin', you know, but everybody has to go their own way, you know.
What was your own reaction... you were in New York when Ornette Coleman came?

I never heard him in person. What he's doing is his own thing, you know what I mean. So, I heard a couple of things that he did and it's his own thing. I mean he had the strength of his convictions and he stuck with his guns and he created something which was his, which is wonderful, you know. Whether the public liked it or not, you know. Whether he was starvin' to death or not, you know.
What about Sonny Rollins?
Well, he come up

up under me just like Coltrane and of course Sonny went into his own thing, you know what I mean. Sonny is an old friend, you know what I mean. But a person has to work hard to create their own identity. And then once you create your own identity then you have to live with that, you know what I mean. That's what that is. According to what's basically in a person's heart, what they want to do. So naturally everybody has their own cross to bear. But you want to create in sound what's you, that's it...as long as it's you. That's the important thing, being yourself.

Supplement to interview with George Big Nick Nicholas
for Institute of Jazz Studies

O.K. Nick, going back over some of the material that we covered earlier and trying to fill in a little more detail on some of these...particularly about the musical environment of your childhood. You've mentioned a number of things that I'd like to know a little more about. Your grandfather was a preacher in Ypsilanti, Michigan.

Yeah. Well, he was a preacher there and I was shiftin' around, 'cause I came from a broken home and I staid with him for a while. But he was a minister and I had to go to church every Sunday. I didn't know too much about it, but I remember they would bring in these gospel quartets and these gospel people; when I look back, church was a nice place to be and, you know, the music. I had an idea of it, but you know, being so young, but I could feel the strength of the church. You know what I mean. So I respected the church.

And that's what happened there. Yeah. It was lively and people were happy to be in church and the quartets were well received and the music was nice and it was beautiful when the spirit was there. But I remember that, you know.
There were traveling quartets that would visit...?

Yeah, years ago, you know what I mean. Like Mahalia Jackson did when she came along. They'd go from church to church and town to town, just like the road shows and the bands and what not, you know. It was another world; it was the religious world. But they had their entertainment too, just like the jazz, you know.
Of your own relatives, who would you

go to church with? Well, I would go with my grand-mother and grandfather. That's the only ones I was with and, of course, I didn't know anybody else, you know, I don't remember the names, you know what I mean. No other relatives that I know of.
You mentioned that you found out some years later that your mother had had a little bit of "professional experience" as a singer.

Yeah, well briefly. She told me... she didn't say too much...she said she had a chance to go to Europe with Ethel Waters, or travel in this country. And I knew that she had a beautiful voice, a beautiful voice. And
I think my voice I inherited from her. And she said she did nightclubs and ... but she gave it up. But she always had a love for music.
Would she sing around the house when you were around?
Oh yeah. Beautiful, beautiful, gorgeous.
What kind of songs would she sing?

Oh, songs of the day...naturally, the old songs. Like she would sing "Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out" and "I Ain't Got Nobody" and things that Bessie Smith did. Then later on, in the '30's, when I was around her she used to sing things that, you know, Bing Crosby did and, you know, things like that. Kate Smith, you know.
Now, you spent just about a year, I guess it was, in Charlestown, South Carolina, and one of the things that particularly struck me was your mention of the Jenkins' Orphanage Band...

Well, they came around every Saturday and we all enjoyed it 'cause they sounded good and they'd pass the hat. They'd come in each neighbourhood and play and it was a happy time for young people. And then the older people, they liked 'em, everybody loved the Jenkins' Orphanage Band. But I remember them.
What kind of instrumentation did they use?
Well they'd have trumpets, trombones, saxophones, clarinets, the drums and they played good.
Do you remember having any particular liking for the saxophones that you would hear at that time?
No, no, they didn't strike me.
Then you mentioned that you started listening to the radio in 1936, programs from New York.

Yes. I started listening to... I'd hear Cab and...particularly Cab. There'd be other bands, but his band stood out because of Chu Berry, the tenor player. And I was playin' tenor then; I 'd just started playin' tenor and he was very outstanding and he had a beautiful tone, marvelous technique and beautiful ideas and he was featured. You could tell that he was Cab's favorite and he was marvelous.
People that you were friendly with, perhaps

even people that you were later to go into Sy Jenkins Band with,
were they also listening to these radio programs?

Oh sure, oh sure. We all listened.
And Count Basie, we listened to Count all the time, you know.
'Cause he was comin' from the Savoy and of course Herschel
Evans and Lester Young, you know. That was the talk of the
country. And of course the records came out...
Did your father have a record player?

No, not at that time, we just had
a radio. But later on, when we moved on the other side of town,
he got a record player.

Did you have any friends that had record
players and do you remember...?
Well Howard Brockington, he had a record player. They had everything.
What kinds of records were they buying?
Well, in those days, you know, he didn't want to be outrageous so he would buy Fletcher Henderson, you know, and of course he'd buy Basie and, you know. He was my best friend when I was a young man.
And he was a member of that first band that you were in, is that right?
Yeah. Sy Jenkins, yeah.
Then, in that area at the time, or perhaps a little bit later, there were some other people who later went
on to make names for themselves in the music.

Well,we had a guy come in from... I don't know where Goofus Carnell come in from...but Chauncey Johns came to my hometown. He was from Kansas City and he was a suave, debonair type person. He played piano. And he started to be friendly with a woman there that was well off and he staid around for a while. So he decided to form a band and so he got us together and we played a few jobs. We played Idlewilde, Michigan, and then...we didn't do too much. But Sy Jenkins and myself and Howard went up to Idlewilde, Michigan, for a summer and then...I don't know how this happened...oh yeah. This Goofus Carnell, he was an old-time carnival man and he got us together and that's how we went to Cincinatti. Hartley Toots was the leader; he was a Southern-Territorial-Band-type man. Then we worked the Cotton Club (in Cincinatti) and Hank Jones and Thad
Jones...
Was Elvin on the scene then...?

No, he was a little baby then. But they were in the band and that's how we went to Cincinatti. That's the first time I ever heard Howard McGhee. He came down from Milwaukee with Leonard Gay's band and...Leonard Gay played nice tenor...but Howard was outstanding. He was playing, I'll never forget, his feature was "Body and Soul" and he was playin' like Roy Eldrige at the time. And last time I was in New York, I was on the radio, and he called in and I took him on back, you know. He says, "you start talkin' about those old days..."; I says, "Yeah, wait a minute," I says, "I'm just playin' w[h]ich ya, Maggie," ('cause you know everybody got a nickname), I says, "when I came to Cincinatti, you were there with Lucky Gay from Milwaukee and
your feature was 'Body and Soul*', I says, "I wasn't but 16, but you were grown." I says, "But Maggie I'm just playin' with you."
(laughter)

I was with Jimmy Lucky in Grand Rapids and he was a trumpet player out of Chicago and he came up there and there was a guy named Maurice Palmer and we had a little band. And Bernie Peacock, who was a friend of mine, a very famous alto player, later on. And a little drummer was around there and he was playin' drums and his name was Wilbur Ware. Yeah, that's where I met him. He was playin' drums, just a kid. And I saw him in New York several times and I says, "You know I remember you," and so we laughed about that. But Bernie Peacock became quite prominent. He was with Lucky Millender and different bands. A very fine alto player.
[D.F.: Who were some of the first singers that you listened to and were influenced by?]

From my mother, you know, I became aware of the female voice. But I wasn't really listening to singers until I went in the Club Congo and these featured singers would come in from...and be guest artists during the week. You know, every week they'd have a different show. The first real singer that I really listened to and fell in love with was Billie Holiday. 'Cause when I was in Saginaw at the Sunshine Gardens, we had a situation there where we had the record player and what not and we listened to Billie. This one woman that lived there, she had all of Billie's recordings and that's when I became aware...because she had Lester and all these guys and Roy and all these people on there. But I really fell in love with Billie Holiday's voice.
When would that have been now?
You first heard her through recordings or on the radio?
No, no. Through recordings.
What are some of the major differences that you are aware of between the music scene when you were young and the way things are now?

Well, I feel that in the older days the musicians were like brothers and -- in fact -- all entertainers, you know, they were like one. And they were more interested in sound and having a good feeling. Whereas today I feel that a lot of people are projecting their own ego and projecting themselves, rather than having a really true, deep

respect for sound and the feeling of sound...of an inception (?) which is to make other people happy. In other words, instead of putting hate in your music and animosity and this tremendous ego trip that people go on. That takes away from the original feeling that I was raised with. And I feel that that should come back. Because if a person goes off into a thing that has no basic relationship to the interrelationship between human beings and human spirits on a day to day basis. And to get away from that and to isolate themselves into a particular syndrome or whatever, I think that takes away. You lose that basic feeling and I can feel when people...I mean, if I'm around people, they have records, they love music, and I can see the effect of certain music on them. You know it's alright to have thinking music, to make you think. But you got to remember, you still have a heart and you still have feelings. You're not supposed to ignore those things. There's no escape. ... I feel that people should... the basic elements of life, if we could come back to that and

have your feet on the ground again and the values that we have of respect for your fellow human being and try to help each other spiritually and mentally from your heart. I think that music--jazz--will become really popular again.

I wish that the day will come that there will be once again genuine joy in living, genuine joy in playing your instrument and genuine joy in singing and a genuine joy period. I'll be glad when that comes back.

O.K., moving ahead a little bit, just to fill in, when you first came to New York, you staid in the Cecil Hotel. I wonder just what the scene was like, if you could say a little more about that: who else was staying there and what kind of things were going on, especially...
Well anybody would be subject to be staying there, you know. It's whoever was in town. But, you know, you could eat there...you could eat downstairs, they

had restaurants. And the main thing was that every night there was a jam session. And, if you were off, and naturally you staid upstairs, you come downstairs and you might see anybody there. There was Don Byas and Lester and Dizzy and Eddie Lockjaw Davis, Paul Gonzalves. You can name 'em. All the guys were there all the time. So every night was a different night. It was stimulating.

You were in an interesting position because you came to New York first and worked there for a while, staid in the Cecil Hotel and then, right after that, you went with Tiny Bradshaw back to Chicago, in the Rum Boogie, and I just wonder if anything by way of contrast with the two scenes, at that time Chicago and New York,/struck your attention.
Well, Chicago's like the Wild West. You know, people played from their heart but it wasn't that sophis-

tication that you get, musically, in New York. I mean everybody played good, everybody, but it was like it was the West, you know what I mean, and everybody played wide open. They played good but it didn't have that artistic sophistication that New York has, you know what I mean. Everybody was happy, but they didn't have that New York sophistication.
Then, in addition, there was your contact with Latin music in New York and I wonder if you could say a little more about that.

Well, every relief band in New York at the time, no matter where you were working. If you were working at a big night club, it was a Latin band. So you had to hear 'em. And, gradually, you heard things that you liked and Machito, he was the first one to actually blend jazz. Because Mario, the trumpet player, he was like the musical

director of the band; he used to be with Chick Webb. He was a trumpet player in Chick Webb's band. So natrually he had that jazz feeling in him. And I know at one time, they were doing the Apollo, Machito, then they would have a jazz saxophonist with 'em. I remember one day, who was that there...I auditioned and Stan Getz auditioned and, I think it was Brew Moore, we all auditioned the same day to do this week in the Apollo with Machito's Latin band. That's how popular the marriage became at that particular time. So it's been an off and on marriage for years. Then Bird made some recordings for Machito, for Norman Granz, you know, Latin things. Then Flip Phillips did some things and Chico Farrell did some things for Cozy Cole when I was with the band, on the Candy label. They were never released. I don't know, they may have been, but I never heard anything about them. But Chico, you know, he's a very famous name today. So I love Latin music, because you know I was exposed to it when I
first came here. Like you get off the bandstand, playin' them shows, Ethel Waters and the chorus girls and what not and then the Latin band would come on. And I liked the music; it's pretty music.
What were some of the other places; you mentioned the Apollo had a regular thing for Latin music. Where else could one regularly go?

If you had money, you go down town to the Orpheum Madrid and all those East Side places, you know what I mean. That wasn't my circle, you know what I mean, tourists and people that went for that and people that had plenty of money.
Aside from Chano Pozo, who you've spoken of earlier, did you work with other Latin musicians?]

Chico Farrell, you know, the arranger. I became quite friendly with him. That is to say he made some arrangements for Cozy Cole, as I said. We recorded them and I got to know him and he's a great arranger.
What was/some of the material that you worked on with him?

Oh, I don't remember the names of the songs. You know, the records got lost, you know what I mean. But when Bossa Nova came through, then it rekindled everybody's interest, because that's such pretty music.
What's your first memory of Bossa Nova coming in?

Dizzy coming back from South America talking about this beautiful music and then Donald Byrd, what's his name, Charlie Byrd went down there and he did some things down there. Then, naturally, Stan Getz made the two recordings and they were a big hit: "The Girl from Ipanema", especially, and "Desafinado". It's marvelous really music. I'm sorry it didn't become popular in this country. I think if the American public could have learned to dance to it, that would have been wonderful, because it was just made for jazz musicians.

I know that in recent years you've taken to singing a good number of Louis Armstrong and you've always had very good things to say about him. I wonder what is your memory of the first...of your first hearing of Louis Armstrong, perhaps your first contact with him and how that progressed over the years.

Well, you know, guys in my hometown... the trumpet players in my hometown...they had Louis' recordings, but it didn't really strike me, because--you know--I was so wrapped up in saxophone. But, as I grew older and I became close to the men, he became larger than life. Then I began to realize, I began to listen to his tone and I found out that his tone was the most beautiful and clear than anybody else's. Because, you know, when you get older you become conscious of your sound and what not, then you listen to him and when you finally see him in person and hear him, then you realize that he is the king. Because he had the biggest, most beautiful sound and it went all through you.
When did you first see him in person?
Oh, let me see. Actually, I first

actually saw him in Detroit, when I was there with Dizzy, in person. He was just getting this band together with this sextet, with Teagarden and Earl Hines and Syd Catlett and Arvil Shaw. That's when I first heard him in person. But they were just gettin' together and I didn't really...it didn't really strike me, you know. Oh, in 1946 he was workin' at a place, he had a big band, but I was workin' down town and I went up there one night, but I was only in there for a few moments, so I didn't really get to it. But Timmy Rogers says, "Nick, Louis. Louis is it Nick," he says, "Listen to him." So, you know, different times...but then when I really got to really hear him was I worked with him in Providence, Rhode Island, at the Celebrity Club and I happened to be in all week long and observed the man. And what I found out then was that that was the biggest most beautiful sound I'd ever heard. You know, you talk about Gabriel, I mean he actually sounded like Gabriel, if there ever was a Gabriel. And then he was the way he was with his

discipline. He was on the bandstand first and he kept his instru- ments clean and then in the afternoon I'd go by the hotel and he was very humerous. He took care of his teeth, he took care of himself. He had one case was for his trumpet and the other case was for his medicines. You know, he had a remedy for everything. So I says, "Well;", then that stuck with me. And then, naturally, after I got indoctrinated, then every time he would play in there, if I got a chance I would go to hear him. And it was the same thing. I caught him at the Paramount and I caught him at dif- ferent places: Bop City and it was the same thing. Then I realized what sound really meant, you know.
This week at the Celebrity Club in Providence, when was that, what year would that have been? Do you remember?
Oh, let's see. Around '56.

He was so warm, his tone was so warm and his personality was so warm, it was recognized and he touched people all over the world. He had that magic and nobody could take it away from him. He was just that warm. And I realized that he lived the life, sincerely, from the heart.
'56 was the year that he did a tour in Ghana.

Yeah. I saw that movie. I went to see that movie. [Edward R. Murrow] he narrated that movie. Well, I kept my eye on Louis ever since, you know, and the closer I got to him I realized how wonderful he was. Truly a wonderful person. Dedicated. You, know, really truly dedicated. I think he contributed most to jazz, as far as the world is concerned. As far as recognition throughout the world is concerned. You know, when I realized his contributions since 1921

and '22 and '23 and how good he sounded then and how big and beautiful his notes were then. And now I've heard some of those things recently and they've updated with--what is it-- the chemistry, I don't know, the texture, the mixture of the records. They've updated it and it sounds just like you were there in 1924 and '25 and '26. That's marvelous. You get the same feeling and everything.
Now, you mentioned just briefly before on the other tape, having played at Birdland. But I wonder if you could say a little more about that: who did you work with there?

I worked there with Milt Buckner one time, on a Monday. Then I had my own band in there a couple times on a Monday. Then I worked there a couple of times and did a week. But, you know, Birdland was the place.
Everybody worked there. And they named it after Charlie Parker, Birdland, you know.
When you say you had your own band in there...?
Quartet.
...who was in that?
Well, let's see. Jackie Byard, and Harold Baker and at one time I had Ronnie Matthews, piano player. Let's see, who else did I have in there. I don't remember, really, all the other guys.
What years...?
Well, that was during the '50's.

Well certainly, as we've gone through the years, in amany ways the high point and, as you said yourself, what you're known for in New York, was the years at the Paradise. And you've mentioned in describing those years a lot of the people who played with you there and some of the people who visited and sat in, people who were prominent at that time. But, in addition, we know that there were in the audience a lot of people who you may have known nothing about, at the time, or who you may have known very little about, but who later went on to become quite prominent and who remembered you. Of course the most famous was John Coltrane.
Yeah, well John Coltrane of the new, younger fellows. Well Coltrane used to come in there with

Red Garland and Philly Joe Jones and John Acee, who was from Philadelphia, and Coltrane was around there (Phil.) for many years. And he used to sit up under me and look at me and he never said nothing. So I says, "Acee, who is that?" He says, "That's John Coltrane," he says, "He plays alto. He plays like Bird." I says, "Yeah?" He says, "Man, he's next to bird."

Then I didn't know at that time that...later on, then I didn't see him anymore. But then I found out that he went with Johnny Hodges and played tenor with him and he worked with Earl Bostic and played tenor with him, learning all the time. And he studied everybody. But I didn't know he was really listening to me.
I guess he was listening to you enough at the time to have warranted his naming quite a well known tune after you.

Yeah, well that was a surprise to me and I went over to his house to congratulate him and thank him because I thought that was very nice of him, 'cause I didn't think he was listening to me that way. But Coltrane was a very humble person and he listened to everybody and that's why he was able to come out with his own style. Because if you don't have a good foundation you can't build a good house. And he contributed and he was a marvelous saxophone player. And it is a great loss that he's gone, you know, because not only his artistic ability, but himself as a human being.
And who are some of the other people that have given you recognition for the role you played in those years at the Paradise?
I understand that Horace Silvers, when I gave him a break in there, that he's mentioned several

times on the radio that he worked there with me. And he even put it on the back of albums, which I thought was nice. And of course Lou Donaldson was there and Blue Mitchell, he became quite prominent. And I was with Max Roach the other day; they were having Betty Carter Day at the Oval Office in Washington, D.C., it was Betty Carter Day. So Betty remembered the Paradise, 'cause I hired her for eight straight months in the Paradise. She had a hard time because they called her Betty Bebop Carter and the "Bebop" label really hurt her career, for years. They wouldn't hire her, but I hired her for eight months in there. This only happened a couple of weeks ago. And she mentioned the Paradise and she announced my name and the place was packed and they had a movie on her, of her life and what not, and I thought it was just lovely. And at the end she looked down at me and Max and pointed her finger and she says, "See, I told you." And then the audience just fell out. (laughter) Everybody fell out. But Betty is coming in to her own now, you know. Of course Horace has made a lot of

records and he's quite prominent and Lou Donaldson works all the time and Blue Mitchell just died and Hank Mobley used to come in there. Then Sonny Rollins, Sonny Rollins used to come in there. He became quite prominent. And Clifford Jordan used to come in there all the time. And Phil Woods; I saw him out in Denver. He's doing well, you know, he was a young kid. And Zoot Sims used to come up there all the time and we talk. When I see the guys, and McGhee, we talk about the days and laugh, you know. Max and I talked about it last week.
[D.F.: Is there anything you would like to say to sum things up here for the interview?]
Well, in conclusion, I would like to say this, that now that I'm getting older I would like to do what I can in the school system, for kindergarden children on

through high school, the private schools, the colleges, the handicapped children, anywhere I can, that I can try to pass this on, so that the jazz will not die, won't be destroyed. So that's what I'm going to dedicate my life to, other than going all over the world and doing these various jobs, I want to become involved with young children everywhere I go. And that's going to be my thing on the side, the rest of my life.
